NVC / CEAC manual tracker

Consular cases live at the Department of State, not USCIS. The NVC has no public API, so this tracker is an honest manual checklist: fees paid, DS-260 submitted, documents uploaded, Documentarily Qualified, interview scheduled.

Open the NVC / CEAC Tracker NVC / CEAC Tracker — sign-in steps & my case

DOL case status

Employment cases often start at the U.S. Department of Labor — PERM labor certification and H-2B temporary labor certification are checked in the DOL's FLAG system (flag.dol.gov) with the case number your employer or attorney holds. NIPTEI explains what each DOL step means and where your case goes next — USCIS, then the visa interview.

See the worker / employer route

EOIR immigration court case status

If your case is in immigration court, check your hearing date and court address any time on the EOIR hotline: 1-800-898-7180 — enter the A-number. Never miss a hearing: missing one can produce a removal order without you there.

Immigration Court — what to know

Detailed update history & visa trends

A case is not one status — it is a history: filed, receipted, biometrics, actively reviewed, interview, decision, card or visa issued. For visa trends, the Priority Date Monitor explains how to read the monthly Visa Bulletin — Dates for Filing vs. Final Action Dates — and News & Deadlines explains every movement and rule change with its official source. 🛣 What happens next — after you file

1 · Filed — your packet goes to USCIS complete: right edition, right fee, signatures in place.
2 · Receipt notice — USCIS mails a receipt notice (Form I-797C) with your receipt number — enter it in Case Watch and monitor your case.
3 · Biometrics — fingerprints and photo at a USCIS Application Support Center near you.
4 · Interview — for many family cases, an interview at your local USCIS office (or the embassy, for consular cases). We help you prepare.
5 · Decision — approval, or a request for more evidence (RFE), a notice, or a denial — each one has a next step.

How long USCIS usually takes depends on the form and the office — check the official USCIS processing times ↗ (we do not invent times). Got an RFE or a notice? Upload it to the RFE Decoder. Denied? Read If Denied? — deadlines are short, so act fast and talk to an attorney.

3 · File

The same hub carries your case through the National Visa Center and the Department of State: DS-260, CEAC uploads, the affidavit of support, and the embassy interview.

4 · Track

After filing, your case lives here: the Case Tracker translates USCIS status messages into plain English, Case Watch follows your receipt numbers, the NVC / CEAC Tracker follows consular cases, and Renewal Alerts warn you 180 / 120 / 90 days before a card, permit, or status expires — so nothing lapses quietly.

5 · Get the right help

A law student may also help inside your case — supervised only, confirmed by their teacher / clinic director, with the supervising attorney's name and bar number always shown to you.

6 · Stay current

Immigration rules move. News & Deadlines explains every change in plain English — who it affects, what happened and when, what it means for you, an example, and the official source where the information came from — so you can act on facts, not rumors.

Family Filing Guides — Filing for Someone You Love

Most of our clients are not filing for themselves. They are filing for a husband or wife, a parent, a child, a brother or sister, or a fiancé(e) — often in another country, often in another language. These guides explain each family route the way we explain it across the desk in Fort Pierce: who it is for, the exact forms in the order you file them, what documents prove the relationship, what it costs, how long each step takes, what can go wrong, and what to do next. NIPTEI is the platform you file on: we tell you every document needed, gather and check them with you, and submit the complete packet for you. Government fees and rules below are cited to their official sources so you can verify them.

Before you file for someone — read what immigration says about money and debts

Filing for a family member is also a money promise. The Affidavit of Support (Form I-864) is a real, legally enforceable contract; USCIS looks at debts, taxes, and child support in specific ways; and a missed filing fee means no case at all. We explain exactly what USCIS says — with the official source for every claim and a plain-English example — on one page: What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone.

Guide 1 · Filing for a spouse

Who it is for: A U.S. citizen or green-card holder married to someone who needs a green card — whether your spouse is already in the United States or living abroad.

If your spouse is inside the U.S. (entered with a visa, border card, or parole, and is eligible to adjust status): the petition and the green-card application usually go together. The core packet is Form I-130 (Petition for Alien Relative) with Form I-130A (your spouse's background supplement — included with the I-130 at no extra charge), Form I-485 (Adjustment of Status — paper filing, USCIS fee $1,440), Form I-864 (Affidavit of Support), Form I-765 (work permit, optional), Form I-131 (travel permit, optional), and the Form I-693 medical exam by a USCIS civil surgeon. This is exactly the 7-form Marriage & Family Green Card Bundle: Basic $999, Standard $1,799, Premium $2,799 — government fees are always separate and never combined with our fee.

If your spouse is outside the U.S.: you file the I-130 with USCIS first. After approval, the case moves to the National Visa Center for consular processing — see the NVC & Department of State guide. Your spouse interviews at the U.S. embassy or consulate, enters on an immigrant visa, and the green card is mailed after the $235 USCIS Immigrant Fee is paid.

Documents that prove the marriage: marriage certificate; evidence the marriage is real and ongoing — joint lease or mortgage, joint bank statements, joint tax returns, insurance naming each other, photos together over time, and statements from people who know you as a couple. If either of you was married before, you also need the divorce decree or death certificate ending every prior marriage. Documents not in English need a full certified English translation.

What can go wrong: filing on an expired form edition (the I-485 edition dated 09/18/26 is mandatory; the I-864 edition dated 08/24/26 is mandatory), a sponsor who does not meet the 2026 income line (for a household of 4, 125% of the federal poverty guideline is $41,250 — check yours with the Sponsor Qualifier), or a spouse who entered without inspection — that fact changes the route and needs an attorney's legal analysis before anyone files. Married less than 2 years on the day the green card is approved? Your spouse receives a 2-year conditional card, and you must file Form I-751 together in the 90 days before it expires (paper filing, USCIS fee $750) to remove the conditions.

Two money-and-loss answers every spouse should read: the sponsor’s I-864 is a real financial obligation — who can be sued, when it ends, and what happens if the sponsor dies, divorces, or loses a job are answered in Ask NIPTEI — Financial Obligation and on the Money, Debts & Filing for Someone page. And if a U.S. citizen spouse has died — even if they never filed an I-130 — the surviving spouse may still get a green card as a widow(er) by self-petitioning on Form I-360 within 2 years of the death: read Ask NIPTEI — Widow / Widower Green Card, and get an attorney or DOJ nonprofit involved immediately, because that deadline does not wait.

If your spouse abuses you — read this before anything else: you do not have to stay in a dangerous marriage to get your green card, and you do not need your spouse's help, signature, or knowledge. Under VAWA, an abused spouse of a U.S. citizen or of a green card holder can self-petition on Form I-360 (USCIS fee $0) and then apply for the green card — USCIS keeps the case confidential and never tells the abuser. The same self-petition exists for an abused child (Guide 3) and an abused parent of a U.S. citizen (Guide 2). Full page, with step-by-step home examples and the document checklist: Domestic Violence — How to Get a Green Card on Your Own (VAWA). If the abuser is not a spouse, parent, or child — a boyfriend or girlfriend, a sibling, an employer — VAWA does not fit, but a U visa (crime victims) or T visa (trafficking) may. These cases involve legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended — and the choice is yours: DIY ($25 per form), a document preparer (clerical only), a licensed attorney, or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit. In danger now? Call 911 · National Domestic Violence Hotline 1-800-799-7233.

Guide 2 · Filing for a parent

Who it is for: A U.S. citizen age 21 or older filing for a mother or father. (Green-card holders cannot petition for parents.) Parents of U.S. citizens are "immediate relatives" — there is no yearly quota and no Visa Bulletin wait for a visa number.

The route: Form I-130 with your birth certificate showing your parent's name (plus your parents' marriage certificate when filing for a father). If your parent is lawfully in the U.S., Form I-485 can usually be filed with it; if your parent is abroad, the case continues at the NVC after I-130 approval. You — the petitioner — must also file the Form I-864 Affidavit of Support and meet the 2026 income requirement for your household size, or use a qualifying joint sponsor.

What can go wrong: name differences between your birth certificate and your parent's ID (explain them in writing and add supporting records), a parent who entered without inspection, or a prior removal order — the last two need an attorney before filing, not after a denial.

Guide 3 · Filing for a child

Who it is for: U.S. citizens and green-card holders filing for a son or daughter. The category — and the wait — depends on the child's age and marital status: unmarried children under 21 of U.S. citizens are immediate relatives with no quota wait; adult or married children, and children of green-card holders, wait in preference categories under the monthly Visa Bulletin.

The route: Form I-130 with the child's birth certificate naming you as parent. For a child abroad, the case continues through the NVC. Timing matters: the Child Status Protection Act (CSPA) can protect a child who is about to turn 21 from "aging out," but the protection has deadlines — if your child is close to 21, do not wait, and get legal advice on the CSPA calculation for your case.

Guide 4 · Filing for a brother or sister

Who it is for: A U.S. citizen age 21 or older filing for a sibling (the F4 preference category). Be honest with families here: this category has the longest Visa Bulletin wait of any family route — often many years. Filing the I-130 early still matters, because the filing date becomes your sibling's priority date — their place in line. While you wait, the Priority Date Monitor explains how to read the Visa Bulletin each month, and your sibling should not overstay a visitor visa or enter without inspection in the meantime — either can destroy the case the I-130 was protecting.

Guide 5 · Filing for a fiancé(e) — the K-1 route

Who it is for: A U.S. citizen (only citizens — not green-card holders) engaged to someone outside the U.S., who will marry within 90 days of entering.

The route, in order: (1) Form I-129F with proof of citizenship, proof you have met in person within the last 2 years, and a signed statement of intent to marry. (2) After approval, your fiancé(e) applies for the K-1 visa through the National Visa Center and the embassy — medical exam and interview abroad. (3) Your fiancé(e) enters on the K-1 and you marry within 90 days. (4) Your spouse then files Form I-485 to adjust status, with the I-864 Affidavit of Support. Children of your fiancé(e) may come as K-2 dependents. After the green card, a marriage under 2 years old means a conditional card and an I-751 later — plan for it from day one.

If your K-1 spouse abuses you after the wedding: a fiancé(e) who married the U.S. citizen petitioner within 90 days and is then abused can self-petition under VAWA as an abused spouse — see the VAWA page. If you did not marry within 90 days, VAWA does not fit that relationship — get a licensed attorney or DOJ nonprofit immediately to check the U visa and other options.

Guide 6 · Filing for a worker or employee

Who it is for: A U.S. employer bringing or keeping a worker — including seasonal H-2B staffing in hospitality, healthcare, construction, and property management, the work our sister service NIPTEI Staffing does every season.

The route, in order: most employment cases start with the Department of Labor (a labor certification or temporary labor certification proving the job and wage), then the employer's petition to USCIS (Form I-129 for temporary workers, Form I-140 for immigrant workers), then the worker's visa interview abroad or change/adjustment of status in the U.S. Employer filings carry strict season and cap deadlines — an employer who starts after the cap closes waits a full season. Employers use the Employer Door; workers should never pay an employer-side petition fee that the law puts on the employer.

Every family case, the same honest warnings

Entered without inspection, a prior deportation or removal order, a missed immigration-court date, or a criminal record — any one of these changes the legal route and can make a routine filing dangerous. Our Path Finder screens for these first, and red-flag cases are routed to a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited representative — preparers do clerical work only and never give legal advice. Fees: our preparer fee and the USCIS fee are always shown separately and never combined; confirm the current government fee at uscis.gov/fees (Form G-1055) before you pay. No one can guarantee approval — what we guarantee is a complete, correct packet, and if USCIS rejects a packet because we used the wrong form edition or the wrong fee, we fix it free.

People also ask — family green cards

How to get a green card if my husband abuses me? You may not need him: under VAWA, an abused spouse of a U.S. citizen or green card holder self-petitions on Form I-360, confidentially. See the VAWA page.

What is the affidavit of support income for 2026? 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines: household of 2 — $27,050; household of 4 — $41,250 (Form I-864P, 2026). Check your household in the Sponsor Qualifier and read Ask NIPTEI — Financial Obligation.

Can a widow get a green card if her citizen husband died before filing? Yes — the widow(er) self-petition on Form I-360, filed within 2 years of the death. See Ask NIPTEI — Widow / Widower Green Card.

I was a victim of a crime. Is there a green card for that? Possibly — the U visa (Form I-918) protects victims of qualifying crimes who help law enforcement, and leads to a green card after 3 years. See the U Visa & T Visa page.

How much does the family green card bundle cost? Our Marriage & Family Green Card Bundle (7 forms): Basic $999 / Standard $1,799 / Premium $2,799 — USCIS fees are always separate (for example, I-485 paper filing $1,440).

The National Visa Center & the Department of State — Consular Processing, Explained

When your family member is outside the United States, USCIS is only the first half of the case. USCIS approves the petition — then the U.S. Department of State takes over: the National Visa Center (NVC) in Portsmouth, New Hampshire collects the visa application, fees, and documents, and a consular officer at the U.S. embassy or consulate in your family member's country makes the final decision at an interview. This is called consular processing, and it confuses more families than any other part of immigration — so here is the whole road, step by step, the way NIPTEI walks it with you. NIPTEI is the platform you file on through every one of these steps: we prepare the petition, we tell you every document the NVC will ask for, we help you complete the DS-260 and upload clean documents to CEAC, and we prepare your family member for the interview. The official systems themselves — CEAC, the DS-260, the embassy — belong to the Department of State, and we link them so you can verify everything.

Step 1 · USCIS approves the petition
NIPTEI files your Form I-130 (or I-129F for a fiancé(e)) with USCIS. On approval, USCIS forwards the case to the NVC instead of deciding the green card itself, because the immigrant is abroad.
Step 2 · The NVC creates your case
The NVC assigns an NVC Case Number (three letters for the consulate, then digits — for example HAV2015… for Havana) and an Invoice ID Number. These two numbers are the keys to everything that follows — save them somewhere safe, and never post them publicly. The NVC emails or mails a welcome letter to the petitioner. Honest fact: the NVC has no public API — there is no automatic lookup, and anyone who claims to "hack" or auto-track CEAC for you is not telling the truth. Our NVC / CEAC Tracker is a manual checklist tracker for exactly that reason.
Step 3 · Log in to CEAC and pay the State Department fees
Sign in at ceac.state.gov (Consular Electronic Application Center) with the case number and invoice ID. Two fees are paid online through CEAC: the Immigrant Visa Application Processing Fee for each applicant and the Affidavit of Support Review Fee for the case — confirm the current amounts on the State Department's official fees page at travel.state.gov — Fees for Visa Services before paying, because government fees change. Fees are paid from a U.S. bank account and take several business days to clear before the forms unlock.
Step 4 · Complete Form DS-260 for every person immigrating
The DS-260 Immigrant Visa Application is completed online in CEAC — one for each family member, including children. It asks for full biographic history: every address, every trip to the U.S., all employment, all prior visa applications and refusals. Answer completely and truthfully: what the DS-260 says will be compared with your documents and your interview answers, and an inconsistency becomes the officer's first question. NIPTEI prepares this with you question by question — in your language — before anything is submitted, because a submitted DS-260 is very hard to change (the NVC must be asked to reopen it).
Step 5 · Submit the Affidavit of Support and financial evidence
The petitioner uploads Form I-864, Affidavit of Support (edition dated 08/24/26), the most recent tax return or IRS tax transcript, W-2s or 1099s, pay stubs, and an employment letter. The income must meet 125% of the 2026 Federal Poverty Guidelines for the household size — for a household of 4, that is $41,250 (100% / active-duty military: $33,000); a household of 2 is $27,050. Short? A qualifying joint sponsor (a U.S. citizen or green-card holder who files their own I-864) or countable assets can close the gap — assets must cover 3× the shortfall for a spouse or minor child of a U.S. citizen, 5× for most other cases. Check the numbers first with the 2026 Sponsor Qualifier.
Step 6 · Upload the civil documents
For each applicant: passport photo page, birth certificate, marriage certificate (and proof every prior marriage ended), police certificates from every country the applicant lived in for 12 months or more since age 16, court and prison records if any, and military records if applicable. Uploads go into CEAC as clean, complete scans — every corner visible, no fingers, no glare — with a full certified English translation and the translator's certificate for anything not in English. The NVC rejects blurry or partial uploads one document at a time, and each rejection restarts that document's review clock. This is the step where careful preparation saves families months.
Step 7 · "Documentarily Qualified"
When the NVC has accepted the DS-260, the fees, the I-864 package, and every civil document, it marks the case Documentarily Qualified (DQ). DQ does not mean approved — it means the file is complete and the case is in line for an interview slot at the embassy or consulate. How long the line is depends on the post and on whether a visa number is available under the Visa Bulletin for preference categories (immediate relatives of U.S. citizens have no quota wait).
Step 8 · The medical exam
Before the interview, each applicant completes a medical exam with a panel physician authorized by that embassy or consulate — not just any doctor. Results are sent to the consulate directly or brought sealed to the interview, exactly as that post instructs. Vaccination records should be brought to the appointment.
Step 9 · The consular interview
The applicant attends in person with the appointment letter, passport, original civil documents (bring the originals of everything uploaded), photos, and the medical results if instructed. The officer verifies the relationship, the documents, and admissibility, and asks questions that must match the DS-260 and the petition. Possible outcomes: approved; a 221(g) refusal — which usually means "not yet": missing documents or administrative processing, with a sheet telling you exactly what to send; or a denial on a legal ground, which needs an attorney immediately. Our Visa Interview preparation walks through the day itself.
Step 10 · Visa issued, entry, and the green card
An approved immigrant visa is placed in the passport, usually with a sealed packet (or electronic equivalent) that must not be opened. After entry to the U.S., pay the $235 USCIS Immigrant Fee online at uscis.gov so the physical green card is produced and mailed to the U.S. address on file. Enter before the visa's expiration date — it is normally tied to the medical exam's validity. Then read Life After the Green Card — and if the marriage was under 2 years old at approval, calendar the I-751 window from day one.

Questions families ask about the NVC

"USCIS approved my I-130 months ago and I have heard nothing." First find the welcome letter — check the email and postal mail of the petitioner and the applicant, including spam. If the NVC created the case, the letter holds the case number and invoice ID. If more than a reasonable time has passed with no letter, the NVC can be reached through its online public-inquiry form at travel.state.gov — Immigrant Visas, and USCIS can confirm where the approved petition was sent. Bring us the approval notice and we will help you work out which door to knock on.

"My case is Documentarily Qualified — why no interview date?" The NVC does not schedule interviews; the embassy or consulate does, in DQ order, as slots and visa numbers allow. Some posts schedule in weeks, others in many months. Keep your contact information current with the NVC — the appointment letter goes to the email and address on file — and do not quit a job, sell a home, or buy plane tickets until the visa is in the passport.

"Can NIPTEI check my CEAC for me?" CEAC sign-in needs your case number and invoice ID, and there is no API or third-party access — you sign in yourself at ceac.state.gov, and we sit with you (in person, by phone, or by video) and go through every screen together. Our CEAC Tools page explains each status message CEAC shows.

Official sources for this section: U.S. Department of State, travel.state.gov — Immigrant Visas; CEAC login, ceac.state.gov; USCIS Immigrant Fee, uscis.gov — USCIS Immigrant Fee. We are not affiliated with the U.S. Department of State or USCIS.

Professional Coordination — Preparer, Attorney, and DOJ, on One Case File

Most immigration cases need two kinds of work. Legal work — eligibility analysis, waivers, court, strategy when something has gone wrong — belongs only to a licensed attorney or a DOJ-accredited representative. Clerical work — gathering documents, completing forms at the client's direction, translations, packet assembly, mailing, and tracking — is what document preparers do. NIPTEI is built so those two kinds of work happen on the same case file, in the same place, instead of in lost email threads between three offices. NIPTEI is the platform the case is filed on; the professionals coordinate around it.

For clients — find your professional

Find a document preparer on the Find a Preparer page and each preparer's own public storefront. Find a licensed attorney in the Attorney & Preparer Directory — attorneys listed here opt in and show a state bar number you can verify with that state's bar before you hire anyone. Find a DOJ-accredited nonprofit in the DOJ Directory, checked against the official EOIR list of recognized organizations. No invented listings: a professional appears here only when they are real, registered, and — for attorneys and DOJ organizations — verified.

For attorneys — find a preparer to coordinate with

An attorney can link with a document preparer on a shared case: the attorney invites or accepts the link, the client consents, and both professionals see the same checklist, the same uploaded documents, the same case status, and the same message thread. The preparer assembles the clerical packet in the shared workspace; the attorney reviews, signs the G-28, and does every part that is legal work. The attorney stays the attorney of record and stays responsible for the legal judgment — the coordination link never turns a preparer into a lawyer, and the preparer never gives the client legal advice inside or outside the shared file.

For DOJ-accredited nonprofits

A DOJ-recognized organization coordinates the same way within its accreditation level: accredited representatives handle the cases their recognition covers, preparers in the network handle clerical overflow, and complex or out-of-scope matters are escalated to a cooperating attorney — with the client's file, checklist, and history moving with the referral instead of starting over.

How a coordinated case runs, step by step

  1. The client starts in one place. Path Finder route, one checklist, one document vault — whichever professional the client hires first, the file starts here.
  2. The safety screen runs first. Entry without inspection, a prior removal order, a missed court date, or a criminal record flags the case as red-flag. Red-flag cases are routed to an attorney or DOJ representative before any filing — a preparer alone never files them.
  3. The link is made. The attorney (or DOJ representative) and the preparer are linked to the case with the client's consent. Each sees only their own assigned clients' files.
  4. The preparer builds the packet. Documents gathered and checked, forms completed at the client's direction, certified translations arranged, packet health check run — correct 2026 editions, correct fees, everything signed where a signature is required.
  5. The attorney does the legal work. Eligibility and waiver analysis, the G-28 notice of appearance, legal argument, RFE/NOID strategy, and representation before USCIS or the court — the parts that are law, done by the lawyer.
  6. One status, seen by everyone. Receipts, biometrics, interview notices, RFEs, and decisions post to the shared file, translated into plain English for the client — so the client never has to carry messages between their own professionals.
  7. Fees stay clean and separate. Each professional bills their own fee through their own account; the platform never holds client money, and our preparer fee is never combined with the USCIS fee — or with the attorney's fee.

The lines that never move

Preparers are not attorneys and do not give legal advice, choose legal strategy, or represent anyone before USCIS or in court. Attorneys do not delegate legal judgment to preparers. DOJ representatives work only within their organization's recognition and their own accreditation level. Coordination makes the paperwork move faster and the file stay whole — it never blurs who is responsible for what. On this static public page, the coordination workspace itself does not run — linked accounts and shared files come with the live back-end; professionals join today through Attorney Registration and Join Our Network.

People also ask

Can I file my immigration documents online?
Yes. You start, upload, pay, and track online with NIPTEI, and we prepare and submit the packet for you. A few USCIS forms are paper-only (Form I-485, for example) — we prepare them and mail the packet for you, and you still never visit our office.

Do I need to visit an immigration office?
Not ours — there is no NIPTEI office visit. USCIS schedules your biometrics and, for many cases, your interview at a USCIS office near where you live. That appointment is with USCIS, and we help you prepare for it.

Can I file from another state?
Yes — all 50 states. Immigration is federal: the same USCIS forms and fees apply in every state, and your NIPTEI team works with you online wherever you live.

What documents do I upload?
Your checklist is built for your case after the free Path Finder: identity documents, relationship proof, financial / tax documents, and the rest — each item named, with how to get it if you do not have it.

How do I pay?
By card or PayPal, to your professional's own account. Our fee and the USCIS fee are always separate — two columns, never combined — and you can Pay in 3 at no extra fee.

🛣 What happens next — after you file

1 · Filed — your packet goes to USCIS complete: right edition, right fee, signatures in place.
2 · Receipt notice — USCIS mails a receipt notice (Form I-797C) with your receipt number — enter it in Case Watch and monitor your case.
3 · Biometrics — fingerprints and photo at a USCIS Application Support Center near you.
4 · Interview — for many family cases, an interview at your local USCIS office (or the embassy, for consular cases). We help you prepare.
5 · Decision — approval, or a request for more evidence (RFE), a notice, or a denial — each one has a next step.

How long USCIS usually takes depends on the form and the office — check the official USCIS processing times ↗ (we do not invent times). Got an RFE or a notice? Upload it to the RFE Decoder. Denied? Read If Denied? — deadlines are short, so act fast and talk to an attorney.

📬 Why USCIS loves a clean packet

USCIS rejects packets for simple, preventable reasons: wrong edition, wrong fee, blank field, missing signature. A clean packet does not get rejected for those. Our 8-Point Packet Health Check + Pre-Flight Lock stops a packet before it goes out if any of those are wrong: correct edition + correct fee checked twice (I-485 edition 09/18/26 · I-864 edition 08/24/26 · fee checked against Form G-1055 · payment by G-1450 / G-1650 — no paper checks), complete evidence in USCIS order (cover letter, exhibit index, documents in the order USCIS expects), no false documents, ever — and your status explained in honest, plain English, so you stop having to call USCIS to ask what it means.

Sponsor Qualifier — Locked to 2026

This checker uses the 2026 Form I-864P poverty guidelines, effective March 1, 2026. The current Form I-864 edition is 08/24/26, mandatory since October 1, 2026 — USCIS can reject an older edition. Figures below are for the contiguous United States at 125% of the federal poverty guidelines (100% for qualifying active-duty military sponsors).

Signing the I-864 is a legal contract — know what it means first

Meeting the income line on this page is only half of sponsoring. The I-864 you sign is legally enforceable: the immigrant you sponsor — and a government agency that pays them means-tested benefits — can sue you to enforce it, and the duty normally lasts until the immigrant becomes a U.S. citizen or is credited with 40 qualifying quarters of work. Read the full plain-English explanation, with official sources and examples: What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone.

What the I-864 really commits you to →

Check your income

Worked example

Income $25,000, household of 4: the 2026 line is $41,250, so you are $16,250 short. To cover that gap with assets you would need $48,750 in assets at 3× (spouse/minor child of a U.S. citizen) or $81,250 at 5× (most other cases). Countable assets are net value that can turn into cash within 12 months — savings, stocks, withdrawable retirement, real estate, vehicles. Your primary home is hard to count; do not count on it. Other ways to qualify: a joint sponsor who files their own I-864 and meets 125% on their own household, a household member on Form I-864A, or the intending immigrant's own lawful income and assets in some cases.

Read the full Financial Obligation answers

The I-864 duty does not end at this qualifier: who can be sued, what assets count, what happens if the sponsor does not pay, and what happens if the sponsor dies, divorces, or loses their job are answered in plain English in Ask NIPTEI — Financial Obligation and on the Money, Debts & Filing for Someone page — each answer with its official source and an example.

Fee Waiver Screener — Form I-912 at 150%

If your household income is at or below 150% of the 2026 guidelines (household of 4: $49,500), you may qualify to ask USCIS to waive the filing fee with Form I-912. Enter your household size and income above and use the 150% column — or ask us: text (772) 971-6129. A waiver is USCIS's decision, never guaranteed.

All four agencies, tracked in one place

An immigration case can live with four different agencies at different times. NIPTEI tracks all of them together — so you never have to guess which door your case is behind.

USCIS — receipt tracker

Petitions and applications filed inside the U.S. carry a 13-character receipt number (for example IOE0123456789). Use the translator above with the exact status wording from your notice or your free USCIS account, and keep every notice in order — together they are your case's update history.

NVC / CEAC — consular tracker (manual)

After USCIS approves a petition for someone abroad, the case moves to the National Visa Center. The NVC offers no public API and CEAC is manual login only at ceac.state.gov, with your NVC case number and invoice ID.

Open the NVC / CEAC Tracker NVC / CEAC Tracker — sign-in steps & my case

DOL — Department of Labor case status

Most employment cases start at the Department of Labor: PERM labor certification, or a temporary labor certification for H-2B and other seasonal work. DOL case status is checked in the DOL's FLAG system (flag.dol.gov) with the case number — held by the employer or the employer's attorney, because the labor certification belongs to the employer's filing. Ask your employer for the case number and the current step, then read what it means in the worker / employer guide.

EOIR — immigration court case status

Court cases are checked on the EOIR automated hotline: 1-800-898-7180 — enter the A-number to hear the next hearing date, the court address, and case information. Hearing dates and addresses change, so check before every hearing and keep a written log of each call: date, time, and what the system said. Never miss a hearing.

Immigration Court — what to know

Your detailed update history — how a case normally moves

  1. Case Was Received — USCIS has your packet and issued your receipt number. That number is your case's ID from here on.
  2. Biometrics Appointment Was Scheduled — fingerprints and photo. Bring the notice and a photo ID; never simply skip it.
  3. Case Is Being Actively Reviewed By USCIS — an officer has the file. This step can last a long time and is not bad news.
  4. Request for Evidence Was Sent — USCIS paused the case and named exactly what is missing. The deadline on the notice does not move.
  5. Interview Was Scheduled — bring originals of everything you filed, your ID, and an interpreter if you need one.
  6. Case Was Approved — follow the letter's next steps: watch for the card, the oath notice, or the NVC welcome letter.
  7. Card Was Mailed To Me — the green card or work permit is on its way to the address on file.
  8. Case Was Denied — the letter explains why and what can still be done. Appeal and motion deadlines are short — get legal help fast.

Consular cases follow their own history: USCIS approval → NVC case created → fees paid → DS-260 submitted → Documentarily Qualified → interview → visa issued. DOL cases move: filed → in process → certified (or audited / denied) → the USCIS petition. Court cases move by hearing dates, not status messages.

Visa trends — read the Visa Bulletin like a professional

For preference categories, whether you can file — and whether your case can be approved — depends on the monthly Visa Bulletin from the Department of State. Two charts matter: Dates for Filing (when you may submit the I-485) and Final Action Dates (when a case may be approved). The Priority Date Monitor walks you through finding your category and country and reading both charts, and News & Deadlines explains each month's movement in plain English with the official source. Honest note: live trend charts and automatic status checking do NOT work on this static page — they come with the live back-end. Nothing here invents processing times or approval odds: for current USCIS processing times, check the official tool at uscis.gov.

NVC / CEAC Tracker — Manual, By Hand

If your approved petition went to the National Visa Center (NVC) for consular processing, your case continues at the U.S. Department of State — not USCIS. The NVC offers NO public API, and there is no automatic lookup we can honestly offer. CEAC is manual login only at ceac.state.gov — you sign in yourself with your NVC case number and invoice ID.

Your manual checklist

  1. Pay the State Department fees in CEAC
  2. Submit the DS-260 visa application for each person
  3. Upload civil documents (birth, marriage, police records)
  4. Submit the Affidavit of Support (I-864) and financial evidence
  5. Wait for “Documentarily Qualified” from the NVC
  6. Wait for your interview appointment at the U.S. embassy or consulate
  7. Complete the medical exam (I-693 equivalent abroad) before the interview

We help you get ready

Learn & Library

Lawful entry vs. unlawful entry — why it matters

If you entered with a visa, border card, or parole and have an I-94, the standard I-485 adjustment route may be open to you. If you entered without inspection, different pathways may apply — Military Parole in Place, advance parole for some DACA/TPS holders, 245(i) grandfathering (with Supplement A and a $1,000 fee), an I-601A waiver with consular processing, or humanitarian relief such as VAWA, U, T, SIJS, or asylum. These cases need a lawyer or DOJ-accredited representative before filing. Check your I-94 free at the official CBP I-94 site: i94.cbp.dhs.gov ↗.

Interview preparation

Bring your appointment notice, government ID, originals of every document you submitted, and certified translations. Answer only what is asked, truthfully, and bring an interpreter if you need one — interviews can be done in your language with a qualified interpreter. For naturalization, study the civics test that applies to your filing date and bring tax transcripts (5 years, or 3 if married to a U.S. citizen), child-support proof if it applies, and proof you met your I-864 support duties if you were sponsored.

I-485 packet checklist (current rules)

Use only the 09/18/26 edition of Form I-485. USCIS policy PA-2026-05 can deny an incomplete packet without first sending a Request for Evidence — send a complete packet the first time, with the sealed I-693 medical exam up front, the I-864 (edition 08/24/26) with any credit freeze lifted, and the $1,440 paper fee by G-1450 or G-1650.

N-400 Good Moral Character — Nov 4, 2026 policy (PM-602-0201)

USCIS now looks closely at tax compliance, child support (even without a court order), compliance with an I-864 support obligation you signed, and public-benefits history when deciding good moral character. Gather proof before you file.

News & Deadlines

USCIS News & Updates — Plain-English summaries. Always confirm details on the official source linked with each post.

How to read immigration news — the NIPTEI way

Immigration news is written for lawyers, in legal language, and it frightens families who do not need to be frightened — or worse, reassures people it should worry. Every story on this page is rewritten the same way: who it affects, what happened and when, the process step by step, what the government is actually trying to tell you, what it means for you, one concrete example, and the official source where the information came from (uscis.gov, travel.state.gov, ceac.state.gov, or federalregister.gov) so you can verify it yourself. One rule protects you from most bad information: if a post, video, or "notario" cannot name the official source and the effective date, do not act on it. NIPTEI is the platform you file on — and the place that explains the news in plain English next to it.

November 4, 2026

USCIS News — November 2026: work-permit extensions end, small fee increases, and a green-card mailing deadline

1 · Work-permit automatic extensions have ended

Who it affects: People renewing a work permit (EAD, Form I-765) in the covered categories — including adjustment-of-status applicants (c)(9), asylum applicants (c)(8), and H-4 spouses (c)(26).

What happened and when: DHS published a final rule on October 14, 2026, effective the same day (91 FR 65306, FR Doc. 2026-20955), adopting the October 30, 2025 interim final rule without change. The automatic extension of an expiring work permit — up to 540 days while a renewal was pending — is over for new renewals.

The process, step by step:

  1. Renewals filed on or after October 30, 2025 get no automatic extension — your card is valid only until the date printed on it.
  2. You may file your renewal up to 180 days before your card expires — file as early as you can.
  3. Renewals filed before October 30, 2025 keep the automatic extension they already had.
  4. Extensions provided by law or by a Federal Register notice itself — for example TPS extensions — continue as before.

What USCIS is trying to tell you: Do not count on a receipt notice to keep working past your card's expiration date. The receipt proves you filed; it no longer extends your card.

What it means for you: Mark the expiration date printed on your card today and file the I-765 renewal early. If the old card expires before the new one is approved, you may have to stop working until it arrives.

Source: Federal Register — final rule, FR Doc. 2026-20955 ↗ · USCIS Form I-765 page ↗

2 · Small fee increases took effect October 16, 2026 (H.R. 1 fees)

Who it affects: Asylum, parole, TPS, and work-permit filers.

What happened and when: The H.R. 1 fees were adjusted for inflation, effective October 16, 2026: annual asylum fee $102 → $105; Form I-131 parole fee $1,020 → $1,050; initial asylum / parole / TPS work-permit fees $560 → $570; Form I-821 TPS fee $510 → $520.

The process, step by step:

  1. Before you mail anything, check the fee for your exact form on Form G-1055, the USCIS fee schedule, on the day you file.
  2. Filings postmarked on or after October 16, 2026 must carry the new fee.
  3. A filing sent with the old fee is rejected — sent back, not just delayed — and you lose your filing date.

What USCIS is trying to tell you: The wrong amount means rejection. The fee is part of a complete packet, not a detail to fix later.

What it means for you: Double-check the amount for your form and category before you seal the envelope, and keep your postmark proof.

Source: USCIS announcement — FY 2027 inflation increase for certain fees ↗ · Form G-1055 Fee Schedule ↗

3 · I-485 mailing addresses changed — old-address grace ends November 9, 2026

Who it affects: Anyone mailing a paper Form I-485.

What happened and when: USCIS changed the I-485 mailing locations on October 7, 2026. Filings sent to an old address are accepted only if postmarked on or before November 9, 2026; after that, the wrong address risks rejection and loss of your filing date. Only the 09/18/26 edition of the I-485 is accepted — there is no edition grace period.

The process, step by step:

  1. Before you send it, confirm the mailing address for your filing category on the USCIS I-485 page — addresses differ by category.
  2. Use the current edition — the edition date is printed at the bottom of the form — and only the 09/18/26 edition is accepted.
  3. Pay the paper fee: $1,440.
  4. Mail with tracking and keep a complete copy of everything you sent.

What USCIS is trying to tell you: Check the address and the edition before you mail, or you lose your place in line.

What it means for you: If your packet went to an old address with a postmark after November 9, 2026, it risks being rejected and losing its filing date. If you are mailing now, verify the address the same day.

Source: USCIS Form I-485 page — current edition & filing addresses ↗

4 · Weekend deadlines — PA-2026-15 (effective October 23, 2026)

Who it affects: Everyone with a USCIS filing deadline.

What happened and when: Policy Alert PA-2026-15, “Definition of Day for Purposes of Filing Deadlines,” was issued September 23, 2026 and took effect October 23, 2026. It reverses the 2023 guidance on how deadline days are counted.

The process, step by step:

  1. Paper deadlines measured in a number of days — for example, 30 days to answer an RFE or a NOID — still roll to the next business day if the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday.
  2. Deadlines tied to an eligibility event — turning 21, an I-94 expiration — do not roll, even if the day lands on a weekend.
  3. Online filings do not get the extra day at all, because USCIS treats them as received the moment you submit.

What USCIS is trying to tell you: Never plan a filing for the last day if the deadline could land on a weekend. File early, and never assume an online deadline runs until midnight in your favor.

What it means for you: Before you count on a weekend, ask which kind of deadline yours is: a day-counted paper deadline, an eligibility-event date, or an online filing. Only the first kind moves.

Source: USCIS Policy Alert PA-2026-15 (PDF) ↗

5 · EB-5 investor fees jump November 30, 2026

Who it affects: EB-5 investors filing Forms I-526, I-526E, and I-829.

What happened and when: A final rule published September 30, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-20016) takes effect November 30, 2026 and raises the EB-5 fees sharply.

The process, step by step: The postmark date controls which fee applies.

  1. Filings postmarked through November 29, 2026 use the current fees: I-526E $3,675 + $1,000 Integrity Fund fee; I-526 $3,675; I-829 $3,750.
  2. Filings postmarked on or after November 30, 2026 use the new fees: I-526E $7,850 + $1,100; I-526 $7,615; I-829 $5,000.
  3. The new fees include a new $75 technology fee on initial I-526 / I-526E filings.

What USCIS is trying to tell you: The filing date now carries thousands of dollars of difference. When you file is part of what you pay.

What it means for you: Investor filings are attorney cases — talk to an EB-5 attorney before either date, and keep proof of your postmark.

Source: Federal Register — final rule, FR Doc. 2026-20016 (PDF) ↗

6 · November Visa Bulletin — USCIS uses Dates for Filing

Who it affects: Employment-based green card applicants.

What happened and when: For November 2026, USCIS will use the Dates for Filing chart for employment-based adjustment-of-status filings.

The process, step by step:

  1. Find your category and country of chargeability on the Dates for Filing chart — not the Final Action Dates chart.
  2. The only movement this month: Other Workers (all chargeability areas, and Mexico) advanced to July 1, 2022. All other employment-based filing dates are unchanged.
  3. If you were eligible to file in October, you remain eligible in November.

What USCIS is trying to tell you: Check the Dates for Filing chart — not the Final Action Dates chart — for whether you can file. Filing early is not approval: a case can only be approved when its date is reached on the Final Action Dates chart.

What it means for you: If your priority date is earlier than the Dates for Filing date for your category and country, you may be able to file the I-485 now and start your (c)(9) work-permit clock.

Source: USCIS — Visa Bulletin filing charts ↗ · U.S. Department of State — Visa Bulletin for November 2026 ↗

Proposed only — not in effect

A proposal to remove deference to prior USCIS approvals — “Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility,” Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529 — is open for public comment through November 13, 2026. It is a proposal only: nothing changes for pending cases unless it is finalized, and the current deference rule stays in force until a final rule takes effect. Source: Federal Register — proposed rule, October 14, 2026 ↗

This post is general information, not legal advice.

Also this season

September 18, 2026: the 2022 public-charge rule was rescinded and the I-485 09/18/26 edition became mandatory. PA-2026-05: USCIS may deny incomplete packets without an RFE or NOID, and day-counting rules changed October 23, 2026 with no 14-day international mailing extension. October 2, 2026: T-visa bona fide determination work permits. October 26, 2026: CBP One parole reopening, fee-free (Sileiri Doe v. DHS). A proposal to remove deference to prior approvals was open for comment through November 13, 2026 — it is not final, and a proposed H-1B grace-period change is also not final.

🪪 Smart Passport & ID Scan — OCR Auto-Fill

Upload a photo of a Passport, Green Card, Driver's License, or Form I-94. The reader runs in your browser, on this device (open-source OCR) — the image is never sent to a server by this page. How translation works here — read this: your preferred language (saved in your profile above, from your registration) is used for every translation, and every message shows both the original and the translation, with the languages it was translated from → to. Numbers, dates, and prices are never altered by translation. 🛣 What happens next — after you file

1 · Filed — your packet goes to USCIS complete: right edition, right fee, signatures in place.
2 · Receipt notice — USCIS mails a receipt notice (Form I-797C) with your receipt number — enter it in Case Watch above and monitor your case.
3 · Biometrics — fingerprints and photo at a USCIS Application Support Center near you.
4 · Interview — for many family cases, an interview at your local USCIS office (or the embassy, for consular cases). We help you prepare.
5 · Decision — approval, or a request for more evidence (RFE), a notice, or a denial — each one has a next step.

How long USCIS usually takes depends on the form and the office — check the official USCIS processing times ↗ (we do not invent times). Got an RFE or a notice? Upload it to the RFE Decoder. Denied? Read If Denied? — deadlines are short, so act fast and talk to an attorney.

🔔 We will remind you

The system reminds you by text and email, in your language, before it is too late: I-751 at 21 months (2-year conditional green card), N-400 at 3 or 5 years, EAD renewal 180 days before expiry, and green card renewal before your card expires. See your dates in Renewal Alerts. On this static page reminders are shown, not sent — live reminders come with the back-end.

8-Point Packet Health Check

Check each point only when it is truly done. When all 8 pass, the verified filing address & shipping label generator unlocks at the end.

🔍 Automated Consistency Check — Cross-Form & Timeline Gap Auditor

Runs inside this Health Check. It compares the legal name and date of birth exactly as they will be typed on each selected form — I-130, I-485, I-864, I-765, I-131 — and audits the 5-year address history and 5-year employment history for unexplained gaps and overlaps. USCIS cross-checks these against each other and against your I-94 / prior filings; one different spelling or one missing month is a classic RFE.

Name & DOB as typed on each form

5-year address history

5-year employment history

Use “Unemployed / homemaker / student” as the employer for any period with no job — explained is fine, blank is a gap.

Health score: 0 / 8

Verified USCIS Filing Address & Shipping Label Generator

Generated from the client's state, the form bundle, and the delivery carrier. USCIS uses different addresses for USPS vs. FedEx / UPS / DHL — never send a courier package to a P.O. Box. Always re-confirm the address on the USCIS “Direct Filing Addresses” page for your form on the day you mail — addresses change, and the wrong address can cost the filing date.

2026 Zero-Rejection Pre-Flight Lock 🔒

Final packet export stays LOCKED until you confirm all four. This lock exists because USCIS policy PA-2026-05 can deny an incomplete packet without an RFE — these four items are the top preventable rejection causes for 2026.

(a) Electronic payment sheet attached — Form G-1450 (credit card) or G-1650 is in the packet. No paper checks.
(b) 2026 edition dates verified — I-485 edition 09/18/26 and I-864 edition 08/24/26 checked at the bottom of the actual forms in this packet.
(c) Sponsor credit freeze is LIFTED — the sponsor has lifted any credit freeze so USCIS / the background check can proceed, and you have told the sponsor to keep it lifted until the check clears.
(d) Client digital review confirmation SIGNED — the client reviewed the completed packet and signed the digital review confirmation. No export of an unreviewed packet.

Lock status: 🔒 LOCKED — 0 of 4 confirmed

Rules used: I-751 — a 2-year conditional card: you may file starting 21 months after approval (the 90-day window before the 2-year anniversary) and must file before the card expires. N-400 — citizenship at 3 years (married to & living with a U.S. citizen) or 5 years; you may file up to 90 days early. EAD — start the renewal 180 days before expiration; automatic extensions ended October 14, 2026, so file early. Always confirm the current rules at uscis.gov.

⏱ My speed fees — I set my own additional fee for each speed

These are your additional service fees, shown on your storefront and on every form card as [Your fee] until you set them — your fee, your business, your price. They are never combined with USCIS fees. Leave a speed off if you do not offer it.

NIPTEI's own speeds are Standard $0 (included), Rush +$199, and 24-Hour Express +$399. The fees you set here are your own storefront speed fees — they replace NIPTEI's speeds on your storefront. Your business, your price.

Standard — complete in 15 to 30 days · my additional fee $
Rush — complete in 7 days · my additional fee $
24-Hour Express — complete in 24 hours · my additional fee $
Same-Day Review — finished form reviewed the same day · my fee $
Weekend Completion — finished Saturday / Sunday · my fee $

Completion times are your preparation completion time, counted from when you have everything you need from the client — never USCIS processing time, and the client is told exactly that at order.

Toggle the clerical forms you offer and set your own preparation fee per form. Nothing is locked: forms that involve legal analysis (G-28, I-601, I-601A, I-212, I-589, Complex RFE / NOID) stay available to you for clerical preparation — with the legal-analysis warning and a clear attorney option on every one, because an attorney's legal review protects you, your client, and the case. You never give legal advice.

⚖ G-28 · I-601 · I-601A · I-212 · I-589 — nothing is locked; an attorney can protect you

These forms involve legal analysis, and legal help is strongly recommended — but no form is locked on this platform. You may prepare the clerical packet, add the form to a client's cart on Choose a Form, and set your own clerical fee — add any of them as a row in the fee builder below, like any other form. What you may never do is give legal advice: you are a non-attorney preparer, and your work is clerical preparation only.

Get an attorney — an attorney can protect you as the document preparer. Work with a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited representative on these forms: the attorney does the legal analysis and signs the G-28, and their legal review protects you, the client, and the case — while you do the clerical preparation you are allowed to do.

I Want to Be a Lawyer — For Our Clients' Children

If your child wants to be an immigration lawyer, this page is for them — in plain English. The families we help today become the lawyers who help families tomorrow.

En español: Si su hijo o hija quiere ser abogado de inmigración: primero termina la universidad (cualquier carrera sirve), luego presenta el examen LSAT y solicita admisión a una escuela de derecho acreditada, estudia 3 años para el título J.D., y después pasa el examen de la barra de su estado para obtener la licencia. Los costos cambian de escuela en escuela — verifique siempre el precio oficial en la página de cada escuela y busque becas y clínicas gratuitas.

An Kreyòl: Si pitit ou vle vin avoka imigrasyon: anvan tout bagay li fini inivèsite (nenpòt matyè bon), apre li pase egzamen LSAT la epi li aplike nan yon lekòl dwa ki akredite, li etidye 3 ane pou diplòm J.D. a, epi apre li pase egzamen bawo eta li a pou li jwenn lisans lan. Pri yo chanje de lekòl a lekòl — toujou verifye pri ofisyèl la sou paj chak lekòl, epi chèche bous ak klinik gratis.

The rest of this page is in English — use the language bar and 🔊 Listen to this page at the top of the site to hear it in Español, Kreyòl Ayisyen, Français, Português, 中文, or العربية. Numbers, dates, and prices are never changed by translation.

Step 1 · Finish college first
Almost every law school requires a bachelor's degree before you start. Any major works — history, languages, business, science. Speaking a second language (Spanish, Kreyòl, French, Portuguese) is a real advantage for an immigration lawyer.
Step 2 · Take the LSAT
The LSAT is the entrance test most law schools use. You register through LSAC ↗, prepare with free and paid study materials, and your score goes with your application. Fee waivers exist for students who cannot afford the test — ask LSAC.
Step 3 · Apply to law school
Apply through LSAC to accredited law schools: transcripts, LSAT score, a personal statement (your story — including your family's immigration story, if you want to tell it), and letters of recommendation. Apply to several schools, and apply for scholarships at every one.
Step 4 · Three years of law school — the J.D.
Law school is usually 3 years full-time. In your second and third year, join your school's immigration clinic — that is where students do the real work on this very page: helping real families, supervised by a licensed attorney. NIPTEI's Law School Clinic Door is built for exactly those clinics.
Step 5 · Pass the bar exam
After the J.D., you take the bar exam in the state where you want to practice, plus that state's character-and-fitness review. Pass it, take the oath, and you are a licensed attorney — with a bar number of your own.
Step 6 · Come back and help families
Many immigration lawyers started as the child translating at a parent's appointment. When you pass the bar, your NIPTEI Law Student profile can become your Attorney profile in one tap — see “From student to attorney” on the Law Student Dashboard.

What does it cost — honestly

Law school costs are different at every school — public schools usually cost less than private ones, and scholarships, grants, and work can change the real price a lot. NIPTEI will not invent a number for you. Check, for every school on your list:

  • The school's own official tuition & fees page (updated every year)
  • Scholarships and grants the school and outside groups offer — money you do not pay back
  • Student loans — money you do pay back, with interest; borrow as little as you can
  • Free help first: many nonprofits (like the DOJ-accredited ones on this site) and law school clinics help families free or on a sliding scale — a student lawyer-in-training learns there, too

Official starting points: LSAC — Law School Admission Council ↗ · your state bar's website for its bar exam · each law school's own admissions and tuition pages.

How to apply — the short list

  1. Finish (or be finishing) a bachelor's degree.
  2. Register with LSAC and take the LSAT.
  3. Pick 4–8 accredited law schools — include at least one with an immigration clinic.
  4. Send transcripts, LSAT score, personal statement, and recommendations through LSAC.
  5. Apply for scholarships and financial aid at every school, before their deadlines.
  6. Choose, enroll, and in 2L / 3L join the immigration clinic — and register here as a Law Student, free.

Register as a Law Student — Free Law School Clinic Door

For parents reading this

Your child's path does not depend on your immigration case, and starting early costs nothing: good grades, a second language kept strong, and one conversation with a school counselor this year. If money is the worry, read the cost card above — scholarships and public schools are real, and clinics train students by helping families like yours, free. We would be proud to be supervised-by line on your child's first case one day — and prouder when their own name is the one after “Attorney.”

✅ What you CAN do — inside an assigned case

  • Help fill out forms, at the client's direction and your supervisor's instruction
  • Gather documents and check them against the case checklist
  • Build and maintain the checklist
  • Translate documents and messages
  • Do legal research for your supervising attorney / DOJ representative
  • Clerical / preparer work — the same work a document preparer does

The attorney / DOJ representative reviews everything, signs the G-28, and is the one responsible for the legal work.

🚫 What you CANNOT do — ever, on NIPTEI

  • Take a case alone — only work on a case an attorney or DOJ rep assigns to you
  • Give legal advice on your own
  • Tell a client “you qualify” or “you should file this”
  • Sign a G-28
  • Represent a client before USCIS or in court
  • Charge the client, take pay per case, or take a % fee through NIPTEI

If a client asks you a legal question, send it to your supervising attorney / DOJ representative — that protects the client, your supervisor, and you.

👀 What the client always sees

“Your law student helper is [Name], [School, Year], supervised by Attorney [Name], Bar # [___]”

That line appears on the case page, in the Client Portal, and at the top of every message you send a client — so the client always knows you are a student, which school you are from, and which licensed attorney (name + bar number) or DOJ-Accredited Representative supervises you and is responsible for the legal work. If your supervisor is a DOJ-Accredited Representative instead of an attorney, the line names them and their organization the same way.

🏪 My storefront — /p/[your-name]

You get a public storefront too — free to register, $35/month to be listed (your storefront live, found in “Find a Law Student”): immigration.niptei.com/p/[your-name]. It shows your photo (optional), name, law school, year, the badge “School ID verified by [Teacher Name], [School]”, and “Supervised by Attorney [Name], Bar # [___]” in big text at the top — plus your clerical services, languages, consultation modes, booking, and completion dates. Clients who hire you there hire you + your supervising attorney together: the case is assigned to the attorney, and you work inside it. Your storefront stays a draft until your teacher confirms you.

8-Point Packet Health Check & Mailing Label Router

The mandatory pre-flight before any of your direct packets is exported or mailed:

  • 2026 edition dates verified — I-485 edition 09/18/26, I-864 edition 08/24/26; old editions are rejected by USCIS.
  • Electronic payment lock — Form G-1450 (credit card) or G-1650 attached; no paper checks.
  • Sponsor credit freeze lifted — confirmed before the I-864 packet is sealed.
  • Cross-form consistency — legal names and dates of birth match 100% across I-130, I-485, I-864, I-765, I-131; 5-year address and employment histories checked for unexplained gaps or overlaps.
  • Signed translations — every foreign-language document carries a signed Translator's Certificate of Accuracy.
  • Client review signed — the client's digital review confirmation is on file before export unlocks (2026 Zero-Rejection Pre-Flight Lock).

The “Do Not File” Danger Shield

Most websites let anyone pay and file. Ours stops you first. Filing Form I-485 with one of these histories can trigger an automatic denial — or put you in deportation proceedings.

The 5-question safety check

Answer honestly. One “Yes” or “Not sure” locks the DIY and Preparer doors and opens only two: a licensed immigration attorney, or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit.

Why a stop sign protects you

Adjustment of status is not available to everyone. An unlawful entry usually cannot be fixed inside the U.S. without a special waiver or a law like §245(i). A prior removal order can be reinstated. False claims to citizenship carry a lifetime bar with almost no waiver. These are legal questions — a preparer who “just files it” is gambling with your family.

Find a Lawyer Free DOJ Nonprofits

Crisis? If a family member was detained, or you have a court date, read Detained or Urgent Help first — before you sign or pay anything.

The “Real Cost” Totalizer — no hidden costs

Other sites advertise a low preparation fee and surprise families later. Here is the honest, all-in picture for the two main routes — government fees, the doctor, translations, photos, everything. Government fees go to the government — never to us. Verify current amounts at uscis.gov and travel.state.gov before paying.

Inside-U.S. route uses: I-130 paper $675, I-485 $1,440, I-765 with pending I-485 $260 (optional), I-131 $630 (optional) — those two are included in the estimate below as the standard bundle packet — plus certified translations (typical $25–$60 per document) and passport photos (typical $10–$20), shown as a $35–$80 range. Consular route uses: I-130 paper $675, NVC Affidavit of Support review $120, DS-260 $325 per person, USCIS Immigrant Fee $235, plus the same translations/photos range. Preparer fee inside the U.S. is the Green Card Bundle tier ($999 / $1,799 / $2,799); consular preparer fee is the I-130 tier ($299 / $499 / $750).

For preference categories (F1, F2A, F2B, F3, F4), a green card can only be issued when the monthly Visa Bulletin reaches your priority date — usually the date USCIS received your I-130. Immediate relatives of U.S. citizens (spouses, unmarried children under 21, parents of citizens 21+) have no quota wait.

Change of Address Helper — Form AR-11 in 3 minutes

Moving without telling USCIS within 10 days is one of the top reasons families miss interview notices and lose cases. Every noncitizen with a pending case must report a new address within 10 days of moving.

1. Gather every receipt number for every pending case — each person, each case.
2. File Form AR-11 free at uscis.gov (online or by mail) — one for each person who moved.
3. Also update your address on each pending case and keep the confirmation. Sponsors must file Form I-865 instead.

Our AR-11 preparation tiers

AR-11 is in the form directory at Basic $25 / Standard $40 / Premium $60 — or file it yourself free at uscis.gov; the form and the filing are always free.

Open the AR-11 card uscis.gov/ar-11 ↗

Changing your address with the post office does NOT change it with USCIS. Do both.

Life Events Alerts — what can cancel a case

Nobody warns families about these three. Each one has ended real cases — each one is preventable if you know in time.

1 · You moved

USCIS mails interview and decision notices to the address on file. A missed notice can mean a denial for abandonment. File AR-11 within 10 days — see the AR-11 Helper.

2 · You traveled

Leaving the U.S. at the wrong moment can abandon a pending I-485 or asylum case. Run the Travel Safety Check before booking anything.

3 · Your card was “delivered” — but is not in your hand

If tracking says delivered and you do not have the card, act the same day: check with the post office and neighbors, then contact USCIS before the card is returned and destroyed.

Also tell us when…

You marry, divorce, have a child, change jobs (for sponsored workers), or a petitioner or sponsor dies. Each can change which category you are in — sometimes for the better. Text (772) 971-6129 and we will tell you what it touches, and when it is a lawyer question.

Mail Scanner — Letter Decoder

A letter from USCIS, the NVC, or immigration court arrives in dense legal English. Is it routine — or a 30-day deadline? Tell us what the letter says at the top, and we decode what it means and how fast you must move.

Honest limit: on this static page nothing is scanned or uploaded — you pick the letter type printed on your notice. Encrypted photo scanning comes with the live back-end.

Packet X-Ray — Pre-Submission Rejection Shield

Most rejections are tiny clerical errors: a missing signature on page 9, an old form edition, a cropped birth certificate, a fee off by a dollar. Run the X-Ray: check each clerical rule honestly and get your readiness score.

What this is: a clerical and technical check only. It can never say your evidence is “strong enough to win” or that you are eligible — that would be legal advice. It tells you whether the packet is complete and correctly assembled. Check each item only when it is truly done.

Security — How NIPTEI Protects You

Your immigration papers hold your whole life: your name, your birthday, your passport, your family. We protect them like it. This page is our security promise, in plain English — the same rules for every account: client, document preparer, licensed attorney, DOJ-accredited nonprofit, law student, teacher / clinic director, and founder / admin.

1 · Strong password — required, not optional

Every registration must set a powerful password:

  • At least 12 characters
  • At least 1 capital letter, 1 small letter, 1 number, and 1 symbol (! @ # $ %)
  • Never “password”, never “123456”, never your name, never your birthday

The registration form shows a strength meter — red / yellow / green — and registration cannot finish until the meter is green. Passwords are never shown, never emailed, and never stored in plain text — in production they are hashed by Supabase Auth, so not even NIPTEI can read yours.

2 · Email code every time you log in

Logging in is two steps, for every role. After your password, we email a 6-digit code to the email address on your account, and you must enter it to get in.

  • The code expires in 10 minutes and can be used only once
  • Enter the wrong code 3 times and the account locks for 15 minutes — and the founder / admin gets an alert
  • “Remember this device for 30 days” is optional — only if you tick it, and only on your own phone or computer. Never tick it on a shared or public computer.

3 · “This was you?” — login alerts

Every login sends an email to the address on the account: “Someone logged in to your NIPTEI account on [date, time, device]. Was this you? If not, change your password now.” So if someone ever steals a password, the real owner knows within seconds — not weeks later.

4 · Locked after too many tries

5 wrong passwords in a row and the account locks for 30 minutes, and an email goes to the account owner. Nobody can sit and guess passwords forever — the door closes.

5 · Founder / Admin — extra protection

The founder / admin account can see the whole platform, so it is protected the hardest: the email code is required every time (there is no “remember this device” for founder / admin), and the founder / admin password must be changed every 90 days.

6 · Your documents — locked down

Only three people can ever see your documents:

  • You — the account owner
  • Your assigned professional — the preparer, attorney, DOJ representative, or supervised law student assigned to your case
  • The founder

No one else. Not another client. Not another preparer. Not a law student who is not assigned to your case. In production this is enforced by Supabase row-level security: an unassigned professional's account returns zero of your documents — not hidden, zero.

7 · Audit log — every open is written down

Every time someone opens one of your documents, it is written in the audit log: who opened it, when, and what document. Logins, code failures, and lockouts are written down too. Nothing happens to your file in the dark. Try the demo on the Document Vault page.

Report a problem

Think someone got into your account? Got a login alert that was not you? Tell us right away — we will lock the account first and ask questions after.

How DIY works

The line we never cross

We provide non-legal clerical form preparation at your direction. We are not a law firm, we do not give legal advice, and we cannot represent you before USCIS or in court. Cases with red flags — removals, arrests, waivers, asylum strategy — go to a licensed attorney or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit first.

File a Form

You chose the form; we type your exact answers at your direction, run the clerical Packet X-Ray, and hand you a mailing-ready packet (or file online where USCIS allows).

How it works

  1. Pick the form and a tier on Choose a Form — nothing is pre-selected.
  2. You pay and register (Pay in 3 available, no extra fee).
  3. We tell you every document needed and gather and check them with you.
  4. We check the packet — edition, signatures, fee — and submit all of the documents for you.

You get updates by text and email. If USCIS rejects your packet because we used the wrong form edition or the wrong fee, we fix it free. That is a completeness promise — not a guarantee of approval; no one can guarantee that.

Not sure which tier? Text us at (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call

Filing Packet

Everything between “I have my documents” and “it is in the mail”: assembly order, cover letter, payment, and proof.

📬 Why USCIS loves a clean packet

USCIS rejects packets for simple, preventable reasons: wrong edition, wrong fee, blank field, missing signature. A clean packet does not get rejected for those. Our 8-Point Packet Health Check + Pre-Flight Lock stops a packet before it goes out if any of those are wrong: correct edition + correct fee checked twice (I-485 edition 09/18/26 · I-864 edition 08/24/26 · fee checked against Form G-1055 · payment by G-1450 / G-1650 — no paper checks), complete evidence in USCIS order (cover letter, exhibit index, documents in the order USCIS expects), no false documents, ever — and your status explained in honest, plain English, so you stop having to call USCIS to ask what it means.

A plain-English explanation of why clean packets help — NIPTEI is not affiliated with or endorsed by USCIS, and USCIS decides every case.

Packet assembly order (top to bottom)

  1. Payment (G-1450 credit card or G-1650, or check/money order where accepted)
  2. Cover letter listing every form and exhibit
  3. G-1145 e-notification form, if you want a text/email receipt
  4. The signed form — current edition, every page
  5. Supporting evidence in the order the checklist lists it
  6. Certified English translations with the translator's certificate

Mail with tracking, keep a complete copy of everything, and write your receipt number on the outside of follow-up mail. Under PA-2026-05, USCIS may deny an incomplete packet without first sending an RFE — send a complete packet the first time.
