How the $25 DIY door works — in plain English

$25 gets you in. You get the checklist and the teaching, and you file your own form with confidence. Most people then move up to the $99 Review — because one wrong edition, one missed signature, or one wrong fee means USCIS sends the whole packet back, and a trained check before mailing is cheap insurance.

From there, the relationship continues: membership ($9.80/month or $98/year) keeps your full checklists, case watch, and deadline reminders on; add-ons (translation, notary, photos, record retrieval) cover the extras a packet needs; and when life moves on, there are more family forms — and renewals: the I-751 at 21 months, citizenship on the N-400 at 3 or 5 years, and the work permit (EAD) renewed 180 days before it expires.

That is how this platform honestly earns: from the review, the membership, the add-ons, family forms, and renewals — not just from the $25. The $25 is the front door, priced so any family can start.

Red flags — a strong warning, never a lock

If the Path Finder safety check flags your case — entry without inspection, removal order, arrest, prior denial, waiver needed — you get a safety pause and a strong warning, not a lock. These cases involve legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended, and an attorney's legal review protects you, the preparer, and the case. But the choice is yours: you may file alone (DIY, $25 per form), use a document preparer (clerical preparation only, no legal advice), or get an attorney or DOJ representative. No form is hidden from you — I-601 / I-601A / I-212 / I-589 included — every one is shown with its legal-analysis warning, never locked away. If you choose DIY or a preparer on a flagged case, we strongly recommend you also get an attorney to review it — Review $99 per form, Human Review $199.

Run the Danger Shield

G-325R — Biographic Information

Form G-325R is the biographic information form used for the alien registration requirement for certain noncitizens who are not already registered. There is no USCIS filing fee.

Our preparation tiers

Basic $60 / Standard $90 / Premium $120 — see the G-325R card in the directory. You will need identity documents and your address and employment history.

Open the G-325R card View on USCIS.gov ↗

Not everyone must register, and registering has legal consequences for some people. If you are unsure whether the requirement applies to you, ask an attorney or DOJ nonprofit before filing — this is exactly the kind of question a preparer cannot answer for you.

myUSCIS Setup

Your official USCIS online account — where receipt notices, biometrics appointments, and case updates appear. We walk you through setting it up correctly the first time.

Set it up right

  1. Create your free account at uscis.gov with an email you check every day — USCIS accounts are always free; never pay anyone for one.
  2. Add each receipt number to the account so every case shows in one place.
  3. Turn on email/text notifications, and add G-1145 to paper packets for an e-receipt.
  4. Keep your password and security answers somewhere safe — and never share them with a preparer. We never need your USCIS password.

Note: USCIS had a case-status email glitch September 30 – November 3, 2026, now fixed — if you missed an update in that window, sign in and check directly.

Free Packet Check

Before you mail: a human clerical review of your finished packet — signatures, editions, translations, fee, assembly. Free, because a rejected packet costs a family months.

What we check (clerical only)

Current form editions, a signature on every form that needs one, the exact government fee and how it is paid, certified translations, copies that are complete and legible, and the packet in the right order. We cannot judge whether your evidence proves your case — that is legal review, and we will say so.

Start with the self-service Packet X-Ray, then text (772) 971-6129 to book the human check.

Packet Rescue

USCIS sent your packet back? A rejection is not a denial — it is a clerical fix and a re-file. Do not panic, and do not just mail the same packet again.

Rescue steps

  1. Read the rejection notice — it names the exact problem (fee, signature, edition, missing page).
  2. Fix only what it names, with the Packet X-Ray as your checklist.
  3. Keep the rejection notice and the green/yellow sheet on top if USCIS included one — it speeds the re-file.
  4. Re-check any deadline: a rejection can cost you a filing window (I-751, TPS). If a deadline is at risk, talk to an attorney the same week.

Our completeness promise: if USCIS rejects a packet we prepared because we used the wrong form edition or the wrong fee, we fix it free.

You got the letter. Bring it here: we help you organize the response packet — what USCIS asked for, in the order they asked, before the deadline. Organizing paperwork is clerical help; deciding legal strategy is not, and we will tell you when you need a lawyer.

An RFE deadline does not move because a weekend intervenes for online filings, and eligibility-event deadlines do not roll (PA-2026-15). Do not wait for the last week.

Embassies

The interview happens at the U.S. embassy or consulate in the applicant's country. Each post has its own local instructions — read yours after the NVC schedules you.

  • Find your post: the U.S. Department of State lists every embassy and consulate at usembassy.gov — use the post the NVC assigns; you cannot pick a different one.
  • Local rules differ: medical exam panel physicians, document delivery, and interview-day entry rules are set by each post.
  • Bring originals: civil documents and the Affidavit of Support evidence the NVC accepted, plus your passport and appointment letter.

Visa Interview guide NVC / CEAC Tracker

Field Offices & Civil Surgeons

Find the offices and doctors USCIS actually uses — by ZIP code, from USCIS itself.

Civil surgeons (Form I-693 medical exam)

Only a USCIS-designated civil surgeon may complete your I-693, and the sealed exam goes in your packet unopened. Our I-693 booking is free — the doctor's fee of $250–$500 is paid to the doctor. Find a designated surgeon on the USCIS Find a Doctor tool at uscis.gov.

Book free — I-693 card

Field offices & biometrics (ASC)

Your interview and fingerprint appointments are assigned by USCIS based on your ZIP code — you do not choose the office. The appointment notice names the address and date; bring the notice and a photo ID, and ask to reschedule only for a serious reason.

Interview Prep

The interview is a conversation about your own life and your own forms. Preparation is not memorizing scripts — it is knowing your packet cold.

Two weeks before

  • Re-read every form you filed — officers ask from the packet.
  • Assemble originals of everything you copied, plus updated evidence (recent joint bills, photos, tax returns for marriage cases).
  • Practice out loud with the Officer Simulator.
  • Arrange a qualified interpreter if you need one — interviews can be done in your language.

Interview Day — hour by hour

For naturalization: study the civics test that applies to your filing date, and bring tax transcripts (5 years, or 3 if married to a U.S. citizen), child-support proof if it applies, and proof you met any I-864 support duties you signed for — see the November 4, 2026 Good Moral Character policy on the News page.

Interview Day

The day itself, hour by hour.

  • Bring: appointment notice, photo IDs, passports, originals folder, updated evidence, and (marriage cases) your spouse.
  • Security: arrive early; phones and bags are restricted at most offices — travel light.
  • Answer only what is asked, truthfully. If you do not understand, say so and ask for the interpreter — never guess.
  • After: you may get a decision the same day, a request for more evidence, or a notice by mail. Write down the officer's name and anything you are told to send.

Visa Interview

The consular interview is short, factual, and document-driven. Officers decide mostly on the papers — your job is consistency with what you filed.

Bring

  • Passport, appointment letter, and DS-260 confirmation page
  • Original civil documents the NVC accepted, plus the medical exam results (sealed, if the post requires you to carry them)
  • The I-864 Affidavit of Support and the sponsor's financial evidence
  • Answers that match your DS-260 — dates, addresses, and history exactly as filed

CEAC tools Embassies

Oath Ceremony

The last step of the N-400 road: the day a resident becomes a citizen.

  • Bring: your appointment notice (Form N-445), your green card, and any documents the notice lists. Answer the questions on the back of the N-445 about the time since your interview.
  • At the ceremony: you surrender your green card, take the Oath of Allegiance, and receive your Certificate of Naturalization.
  • After: check every letter of your name on the certificate before you leave, then apply for a U.S. passport, update your Social Security record, and register to vote.

N-400 Test Prep

Life After the Green Card Starter

Approval is a beginning, not a finish line. Your first 30 days — and the rules that protect your status for years.

And after citizenship?

When you become a U.S. citizen, a new door opens: bring your parents, spouse, or children, register to vote, and get a U.S. passport.

After You Become a Citizen

First 30 days

  • Get or update your Social Security card.
  • Get a state REAL ID driver's license or ID.
  • Start your citizenship countdown — 5 years, or 3 if married to and living with a U.S. citizen spouse (see Guide: After Getting a Green Card).

Rules that protect the card

  • File AR-11 within 10 days of every move.
  • Trips abroad of 6 months or more can break continuous residence; a year or more can abandon the card — run the Travel Safety Check.
  • Conditional 2-year cards: file I-751 in the 90 days before the card expires.
  • Keep filing taxes as a resident and keep proof — it matters for I-751 and N-400.

Consular & NVC Auto-Pilot — the 1-Click CEAC Formatter

Families get stuck at the National Visa Center for months over file rules: uploads over the CEAC size limit, wrong file types, sideways scans. This checker applies the CEAC upload rules to a document before you upload it.

Honest limits: the NVC/CEAC system has NO public API and CEAC is manual login only at ceac.state.gov — nothing here logs in for you or submits anything. On this static page the file never leaves your device; the checker only measures the file you pick and lists what to fix. It cannot compress or convert the file for you.

CEAC upload rules checklist

  • One document per upload — do not combine a birth certificate and its translation in one file unless CEAC asks for it that way
  • PDF or JPG, upright and readable, every corner visible
  • Keep each file small — if CEAC rejects it for size, re-scan at a lower resolution rather than photographing a screen
  • Name files clearly before you upload (for example: Birth-Certificate.pdf, Marriage-Certificate.pdf)
  • Upload the certified English translation with each foreign-language civil document

Ask NIPTEI — Every Question Answered

Type a word — fee, spouse, interview, denied, work permit — and the answers below filter themselves. Every answer is plain English, names its official source where there is one, and ends with what to do next. Still not sure after reading? Text (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call.

Forms — Which form do I need?

Start with your situation, not a form number: the Path Finder asks 5 questions and names the route and the forms. The most common: I-130 petitions for a relative; I-485 adjusts status to a green card inside the U.S.; I-765 is a work permit; I-131 is a travel permit; I-864 is the sponsor's Affidavit of Support; N-400 is citizenship. Every one of the 107 forms is listed with its purpose on Choose a Form. Source: uscis.gov.

Forms — What does "form edition" mean, and why was my packet rejected?

USCIS forms are re-issued with a date in the bottom corner, and after a deadline only the newest edition is accepted — today the I-485 edition dated 09/18/26 and the I-864 edition dated 08/24/26 are mandatory. A packet mailed on an old edition is rejected and returned unfiled, and the receipt clock never starts. NIPTEI's packet health check verifies the edition of every form before mailing — and if USCIS ever rejects a packet because we used the wrong edition or the wrong fee, we fix it free.

Money & debts — What does immigration say about money I owe, or money my sponsor owes?

The plain-English page: What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone — the I-864 is a real, enforceable contract; what happens if a sponsor does not pay; public charge after the September 18, 2026 rule change; taxes and child support; what happens if a filing fee is wrong or missing. Every claim has an official source and an example. Still not sure? Text (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call.

Before filing — What should I know before anyone files for me?

Two pages, read them first: Before You File — Know Everything In Advance (forms, all the money, all the documents, all the time, all the risks, who does what, after you file — with the printable client checklist) and 15 Things To Know (scams, detention, travel warnings, denials, address changes, children turning 21, priority dates, state preparer rules, and NIPTEI's Do Not File list). Still not sure? Text (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call.

Fees — How much does it cost, in total?

Two separate numbers, always: our preparer fee (by form and tier — for example the Marriage & Family Green Card Bundle is $999 Basic / $1,799 Standard / $2,799 Premium) and the USCIS government fee (for example I-485 paper filing $1,440, I-751 paper filing $750, I-730 USCIS fee $0). They are never combined into one figure. Add the real extras honestly: the medical exam is paid to the doctor (about $250–$500), plus translations and photos where needed. The Real Cost Totalizer adds your whole case up before you commit. Our fee can be split Pay in 3, no extra fee. Source for government fees: Form G-1055 at uscis.gov/fees — confirm before you pay, because fees change.

Fees — Can I get the USCIS fee waived?

Sometimes. Form I-912 asks USCIS to waive a fee for people who receive a means-tested benefit, whose household income is at or below 150% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines, or who show financial hardship — some forms cannot be waived at all. Run the Fee Waiver Screener before you pay anything. Source: uscis.gov/feewaiver.

Family — I am filing for my spouse. Where do I start?

With the spouse guide: inside the U.S., I-130 + I-130A + I-485 + I-864 usually file together (the Green Card Bundle covers all 7 forms); outside the U.S., the I-130 files first and the case continues at the National Visa Center. Either way you must prove a real marriage and meet the sponsor income line. Still not sure? Text (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call.

Family — My family member is abroad. What is the NVC?

The National Visa Center is the Department of State office that takes over after USCIS approves your petition for someone outside the U.S.: it collects the DS-260 application, the State Department fees, your I-864, and the civil documents through CEAC, marks the case Documentarily Qualified, and the embassy schedules the interview. The full road is explained in the NVC & Department of State guide. Source: travel.state.gov.

Family — How much must a sponsor earn in 2026?

125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for your household size: household of 2 — $27,050; household of 4 — $41,250 (active-duty military sponsors of a spouse or child: 100%, household of 4 — $33,000). If income falls short, a joint sponsor or countable assets (3× the shortfall for a U.S. citizen's spouse or minor child, 5× for most others) can close the gap. Check your exact household with the 2026 Sponsor Qualifier. Source: Form I-864P, uscis.gov.

Work — My work permit is expiring. Is it automatically extended?

Not anymore for new renewals: DHS ended automatic EAD extensions effective October 14, 2026 (final rule, FR Doc. 2026-20955). File the I-765 renewal as early as USCIS allows — up to 180 days before expiry in most categories — because a gap can cost a job. Full explanation in News & Deadlines. Source: federalregister.gov.

Travel — Can I travel while my case is pending?

Leaving the U.S. without an approved travel permit (Form I-131, advance parole) usually abandons a pending I-485 — and for some people, leaving triggers a 3- or 10-year bar on coming back. Run the Travel Safety Check before buying any ticket, and if you have any unlawful-presence history, ask an attorney first. Still not sure? Text (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call.

Interview — What happens at the interview?

The officer checks your documents against your application and asks questions that must match what you filed. Bring originals of everything submitted, arrive early, answer truthfully and briefly. Prepare with Interview Prep and the Interview Day walkthrough; for a family member abroad, see the consular interview step in the NVC guide.

Denied — USCIS sent me an RFE, a NOID, or a denial. What now?

Do not ignore it and do not miss the deadline printed on the letter — an RFE or NOID deadline cannot be extended. An RFE means "send more evidence"; the RFE Decoder turns the letter into a checklist. A denial may allow a motion or appeal (Form I-290B) within about 30 days. Complex RFEs, NOIDs, and denials go to an attorney — see If Denied?. Still not sure? Text (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call — bring the letter.

Court — I have a court date, a removal order, or a detained family member

These are legal emergencies, not paperwork: a missed hearing can mean an automatic removal order. Preparers cannot represent you in court. Read Immigration Court or Detained now, and contact a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited representative immediately — find one in the Directory.

Renewals — When do I renew or replace my card?

Green card: Form I-90. Two-year conditional card: Form I-751 in the 90 days before it expires — never after. Work permit: Form I-765, as early as allowed. DACA and TPS follow their own windows. The Renewal Alerts page works out your 180 / 120 / 90-day warning dates.

About NIPTEI — Are you lawyers? Can you guarantee approval?

No, and no. NIPTEI is a document preparation service: preparers are not attorneys, do not give legal advice, and are not affiliated with USCIS or the Department of State. No one can guarantee a petition or visa will be approved. What we do guarantee is a complete, correct packet — and we fix it free if USCIS rejects it because of a wrong edition or wrong fee from us. Cases that need legal judgment are routed to verified attorneys and DOJ-accredited nonprofits you can find right here on the platform.

Why NIPTEI — Why is NIPTEI #1?

We file, we track, we speak your language, we bring your family in, we show you every fee, we do it from your home, and we bring your attorney and your preparer together. The full page lists all 20 Lawfully reasons plus Adopt NIPTEI, the USCIS-ready packet, the G-28 workspace, the DOJ accreditation tracker, the Case Status share link, one case one truth, Sponsor / Family Door, money in two columns, and no office visit required. Professionals — Can my attorney or DOJ nonprofit use NIPTEI with me?

Yes — ask them to Adopt NIPTEI. They send you one link; you upload your documents; they see the same case file, same checklist, and same status — and they file it. Attorneys work in the G-28 workspace, DOJ nonprofits use the accreditation tracker and I-912 queue, and any of them can send you a Case Status share link. Domestic Violence, VAWA, U Visa & T Visa — A Green Card On Your Own

If the person who was supposed to file for you is the person hurting you — or you were the victim of a crime or of trafficking — immigration law has doors that do not depend on that person. These answers are the short version; each one links to a full page. These cases involve legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended — and the choice of help is always yours: DIY ($25 per form), a document preparer (clerical only), a licensed attorney, or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit. General information, not legal advice.

VAWA — My husband or wife abuses me. Can I get a green card without them?

Yes — this is what VAWA is for. The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) lets an abused spouse of a U.S. citizen or green card holder file for themselves on Form I-360 (a “self-petition”) — without the abuser knowing, without the abuser's help, and without the abuser filing anything. The USCIS fee for a VAWA I-360 is $0. USCIS keeps the case confidential and does not tell the abuser you filed (8 U.S.C. §1367). Abused children (under 21, unmarried) and abused parents of U.S. citizens can also self-petition. Do NOT contact the abuser for documents. Full page, with step-by-step home examples and the document checklist: Domestic Violence — How to Get a Green Card on Your Own (VAWA).

Example: a wife whose U.S. citizen husband threatens “I will call immigration if you leave” files the I-360 herself, from a safe address. He is never told. She later files the I-485 and gets her own green card.

Source: USCIS, Abused Spouses, Children and Parents (VAWA) — uscis.gov ↗. In danger now? Call 911. National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 (TTY 1-800-787-3224), text “START” to 88788 — free, confidential, 24/7. General information, not legal advice.

U visa — I was the victim of a crime. Can a U visa give me a green card?

It can. The U visa (Form I-918) protects victims of qualifying crimes — domestic violence, sexual assault, felonious assault, robbery, extortion, trafficking, stalking, and others — who suffered substantial physical or mental abuse and who helped, are helping, or are willing to help police or prosecutors. A law-enforcement agency must sign a certification (Form I-918, Supplement B). There is no USCIS fee for the I-918. U status lasts 4 years, comes with a work permit, and after 3 years in U status you can apply for a green card on Form I-485. Only 10,000 U visas are granted to main applicants each year, so the wait can be long — but a bona fide determination can bring deferred action and a work permit while you wait. Full page: U Visa — If You Were a Victim of a Crime, You May Qualify for a Green Card.

Example: a woman abused by her boyfriend — who cannot file VAWA for her because they never married — calls the police, cooperates, gets the Supplement B signed, and files the I-918. The U visa, not VAWA, is her door.

Source: USCIS, Victims of Criminal Activity: U Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

VAWA / U visa — The person abusing me is NOT my spouse, parent, or child. What can I do?

Read this plainly: VAWA does not cover every abuser. VAWA covers only an abusive spouse, parent, or child who is a U.S. citizen or green card holder (and a K-1 spouse you actually married). A brother or sister, a boyfriend or girlfriend you never married, an employer, or another relative is not a VAWA relationship. That does not mean nothing can help: a U visa (victim of a qualifying crime who helps law enforcement), a T visa (victim of human trafficking, Form I-914), asylum, or another form of relief may fit instead. Which one fits is a legal decision — an attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit must check your facts. Do not guess, and do not pay anyone who guesses. Start with the U Visa & T Visa page, then get the warm hand-off below.

Find a Licensed Attorney Find a DOJ Nonprofit

Source: USCIS, VAWA — uscis.gov ↗; U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Immigration Options for Victims of Crime — dhs.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

T visa — I was forced to work or was trafficked. Is there a visa for that?

Yes. The T visa (Form I-914) is for victims of a severe form of human trafficking — being made to work or provide services, or to perform commercial sex acts, through force, fraud, or coercion — who are in the United States because of the trafficking. There is no USCIS fee for the I-914, T status lasts 4 years with a work permit, and a green card can follow after 3 years. Some trafficking victims also qualify for a U visa — an attorney or DOJ nonprofit checks which fits. The T visa is explained on the U Visa & T Visa page. National Human Trafficking Hotline: 1-888-373-7888 — free, confidential, 24/7, in more than 200 languages.

Source: USCIS, Victims of Human Trafficking: T Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Financial Obligation — For The Immigrant And The Family Applying For Them

When a family member files for you, real money duties come with the paperwork — mostly for the sponsor who signs Form I-864. These answers explain the duty in plain English, with the official source and an example for each. General information, not legal advice. Where USCIS does not state a rule, the answer says so — we do not state a rule as fact unless an official source states it.

Financial obligation — What is the Affidavit of Support (Form I-864), and is it really a contract?

Yes — it is a real, legally enforceable contract, not a formality. When a sponsor signs Form I-864, the sponsor promises the U.S. government to support the immigrant at 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines and to repay the government if the immigrant receives means-tested public benefits. Who can be sued: the immigrant can sue the sponsor for the support promised, and a government agency that paid benefits can sue the sponsor for repayment. When the duty ends — only on one of these events: the immigrant becomes a U.S. citizen; the immigrant is credited with 40 qualifying quarters of work (about 10 years); the immigrant dies; the immigrant permanently leaves the United States; or the sponsor dies (amounts already owed can still be claimed from the sponsor's estate). Divorce does not end it, and losing a job does not end it.

Example: a husband signs the I-864 for his wife. She works for about 10 years and is credited with 40 quarters — only then does his support duty end, unless she becomes a citizen sooner.

Source: USCIS, Form I-864, Affidavit of Support — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗ and the Form I-864 instructions (INA §213A). General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — How much income does a sponsor need in 2026?

The sponsor's income must reach 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for the whole household (sponsor + everyone the sponsor supports + the immigrants being sponsored), from Form I-864P (2026, effective March 1, 2026). 48 contiguous states: household of 2 — $27,050; 3 — $34,150; 4 — $41,250; 5 — $48,350; 6 — $55,450; 7 — $62,550; 8 — $69,650; each extra person +$7,100. A sponsor on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces who is sponsoring a spouse or child needs only 100% — household of 4: $33,000. Alaska is higher (household of 2 — $33,813; household of 4 — $51,563; each extra +$8,875) and so is Hawaii (household of 2 — $31,113; household of 4 — $47,438; each extra +$8,163).

Example: a sponsor in Florida with a household of 4 must show at least $41,250 a year. Check your exact household in the 2026 Sponsor Qualifier.

Source: USCIS, Form I-864P, HHS Poverty Guidelines for Affidavit of Support — uscis.gov/i-864p ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — What if the sponsor does not earn enough?

There are four honest ways to close the gap. (1) A joint sponsor — a different U.S. citizen or green-card holder who files their own I-864 and meets the 125% line for their own household, by themselves. (2) A household member — a relative living with the sponsor adds their income by signing Form I-864A. (3) The immigrant's own income — it counts when the immigrant is legally working in the U.S. and will keep working for the same employer after the green card. (4) Assets — income first, then assets cover the shortfall at 3× the shortfall for the spouse or minor child of a U.S. citizen, or 5× for most other cases. Income and assets can be combined.

Example: income $25,000, household of 4 — the line is $41,250, so the sponsor is $16,250 short. Covering it with assets takes $48,750 in countable assets at 3× (spouse/minor child of a U.S. citizen) or $81,250 at 5× (most other cases). If the Sponsor Qualifier says NOT YET QUALIFIED, use Invite a Joint Sponsor in the Family & Sponsor Workspace.

Source: USCIS, Form I-864 instructions — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — What assets count toward the I-864?

An asset counts at its net value — what it is worth minus everything owed on it — and only if it can be turned into cash within 12 months (assets abroad must also be transferable to the U.S.). Countable: cash, checking and savings; stocks, bonds, and mutual funds; retirement accounts that can be withdrawn; real estate; vehicles and other personal property with real resale value — each with proof of ownership, value, and debts. The home the sponsor lives in is hard to count — it cannot be sold quickly without the sponsor losing their home, and USCIS may not accept it the way it accepts a second property. We do not promise it counts. Borrowed money does not count, and an asset with debts equal to its value counts as $0.

Example: $20,000 in savings plus a paid-off car worth $8,000 = $28,000 of countable assets — measured against the 3× or 5× need in the answer above.

Source: USCIS, Form I-864 instructions — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — What if the sponsor does not pay, or the immigrant needs help?

If the immigrant receives a means-tested benefit (a public benefit based on low income), the agency that paid it can demand repayment from the sponsor — and sue if the sponsor refuses. The immigrant can also sue the sponsor directly for the support the I-864 promised. And when the immigrant applies for benefits, the sponsor's income is usually “deemed” to the immigrant — counted as if it were the immigrant's own income — which can make the immigrant ineligible for the benefit in the first place. Signing the I-864 and then ignoring it is not an option; the duty is real until one of the ending events in the first answer on this page.

Example: a sponsored immigrant receives a means-tested cash benefit for 6 months. The agency bills the sponsor for what it paid — the sponsor owes the agency, not the immigrant, for that repayment.

Source: USCIS, Form I-864, Affidavit of Support — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗ (INA §213A). General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — Does the sponsor owe money for the immigrant's debts, taxes, or child support?

Three different things — do not mix them up. (1) The immigrant's private debts: the I-864 is a promise to support the immigrant and to repay means-tested benefits — it is not a promise to pay the immigrant's credit cards or private loans. (2) A sponsor who owes money: USCIS does not publish a rule that a sponsor who owes debts is automatically disqualified — for the I-864, what counts is the sponsor's income and assets against the 125% line. Where USCIS does not state a rule, we say so rather than guess. One real duty: the I-864 makes the sponsor show tax returns, so a sponsor who has not filed a required return must fix that first. (3) The sponsor's own citizenship later: unpaid taxes and unpaid child support can be held against a person who applies for citizenship on Form N-400, under Good Moral Character — USCIS's policy memo of November 4, 2026 (PM-602-0201) addresses exactly this. That is an N-400 rule, not an I-864 disqualification.

Example: a sponsor earns $45,000 for a household of 4 and owes $3,000 on a credit card. The debt alone does not disqualify the I-864 — the $45,000 income is above the $41,250 line. But if that same sponsor later files N-400 while ignoring a tax bill or child-support arrears, the citizenship case is where it can hurt.

Sources: USCIS, Form I-864 — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗; USCIS Policy Manual update PM-602-0201 (Nov 4, 2026). See also What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone. General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — Who pays the USCIS fees and the preparer fees?

Two separate columns, never combined. USCIS government fees are paid to USCIS — for paper filings, electronically with Form G-1450 (credit/debit card) or Form G-1650 (ACH bank transfer); USCIS no longer takes paper checks or money orders for these filings. Anyone may pay a fee (the immigrant, the sponsor, or family helping), but the fee belongs to the case it is filed with. A wrong or missing fee means rejection — no receipt number, no case, no protected filing date. And USCIS keeps its fees even when a case is denied: filing fees are not refunded just because a case is denied — refunds are narrow, such as a USCIS error. Our preparer fees are paid to NIPTEI or your professional, always shown in their own column (for example, the Green Card Bundle $999 / $1,799 / $2,799 is a service fee — the I-485 USCIS fee of $1,440 paper is separate).

Example: a bundle client pays $1,799 to NIPTEI (Standard) and $1,440 to USCIS for the I-485 — two payments, two columns, never one combined number.

Source: USCIS, Form G-1055, Fee Schedule — uscis.gov/fees ↗. Confirm every fee there before you pay, because fees change. General information, not legal advice.

Financial obligation — What happens if the sponsor dies, divorces, or loses their job?

Divorce: the I-864 duty does not end — a divorced sponsor still owes the support promised until an ending event happens. Job loss: the duty does not end either — the promise was made to the government, not to an employer. The sponsor dies: the duty ends going forward (amounts already owed can be claimed from the sponsor's estate). The petitioner dies before the immigrant gets the green card: that is different and urgent — the case usually cannot simply continue; in some cases a substitute sponsor (a close relative) can be accepted so the case survives, but that is legal work with deadlines. If a petitioner or sponsor has died, talk to an attorney or DOJ nonprofit immediately — do not wait and do not guess.

Example: a couple divorces a year after the green card. The sponsoring ex-spouse still owes the I-864 support duty — the divorce decree does not cancel the contract with the government.

Source: USCIS, Form I-864 instructions — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗ (INA §213A). General information, not legal advice.

Widow / Widower Green Card — If Your U.S. Citizen Spouse Died

If your husband or wife was a U.S. citizen and died before they ever applied for you, you may still be able to get your green card. These answers explain the widow(er) route in plain English, with the official source and an example for each. This case involves legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended — and the choice is yours: you may file alone (DIY, $25 per form), use a document preparer (clerical preparation only — Form I-360: Basic $599 / Standard $750 / Premium $900), or get an attorney or DOJ representative. If you choose DIY or a preparer, we strongly recommend an attorney review as well — Review $99 per form, Human Review $199. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — Who qualifies for the widow(er) green card?

You may qualify if you were married to a U.S. citizen who died, you were not legally separated when your spouse died, and you have not remarried. Two facts surprise most people: it is OK if your spouse never filed an I-130 for you — no petition needs to exist — and it is OK if you were married less than 2 years. The widow(er) files for themselves (a “self-petition”) on Form I-360, and USCIS treats an approved widow(er) as an immediate relative — there is no yearly quota wait for a visa number.

Example: a woman married a U.S. citizen 14 months ago. He died suddenly, before filing anything. She can still self-petition on Form I-360 — the short marriage and the missing I-130 do not block her.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — What form do I file, and in what order?

Step 1 — Form I-360, the widow(er) self-petition. USCIS lists no filing fee ($0) for a widow(er) of a U.S. citizen on Form I-360 — confirm on Form G-1055 at uscis.gov/fees before you file, because fees change. Step 2 — the green card itself: if you are inside the U.S., file Form I-485 (paper filing, USCIS fee $1,440 — it can be filed with the I-360 or after approval); if you are outside the U.S., your case continues through the National Visa Center and the embassy (consular processing — see the NVC & Department of State guide). One relief built into this route: widow(er) self-petitioners do not need an Affidavit of Support (Form I-864).

Example: a widower living in Florida files the I-360 together with the I-485. A widow living abroad files the I-360 first, then finishes at the NVC and her embassy interview.

Sources: USCIS, Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗ and Form G-1055 — uscis.gov/fees ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — What is the deadline? What if I miss it?

The Form I-360 must be filed within 2 years of your citizen spouse's death. That deadline is strict. If the 2 years have already passed, the widow(er) self-petition is no longer available — but do not assume nothing can be done: a different route may exist for your facts, and only an attorney or DOJ-accredited representative can tell you. If the deadline is anywhere close, contact an attorney or DOJ nonprofit immediately — this month, not this year.

Example: your spouse died in March 2026. Your I-360 must reach USCIS by March 2028. A family that waits until April 2028 has missed the widow(er) door.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — What documents do I need?

The core evidence: (1) proof of the marriage (marriage certificate); (2) proof your spouse was a U.S. citizen (U.S. passport, U.S. birth certificate, or naturalization certificate); (3) your spouse's death certificate; (4) proof the marriage was real — joint lease or accounts, tax returns filed together, insurance, photos over time, statements from people who knew you as a couple; and (5) your own identity documents, with a full certified English translation of anything not in English. Missing a document? Do not give up and do not invent one — order a certified copy from the office that issued it, and if a record truly cannot be obtained, an attorney can advise on the secondary evidence USCIS accepts.

Example: a widow cannot find her late husband's naturalization certificate. A certified copy can be requested, and his U.S. passport can prove citizenship in the meantime — an attorney confirms which proof USCIS will accept in her case.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 instructions — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — Can my children get green cards too?

Yes — your unmarried children under 21 can be included with your widow(er) case and immigrate with you. Two warnings. Your children must stay unmarried to remain included. And a child who is anywhere near 21 is a deadline case: the Child Status Protection Act (CSPA) protects children in many immediate-relative cases, but the calculation is legal work — file now and have an attorney check the CSPA math rather than risk a child aging out.

Example: a widow files her I-360 with her 19-year-old unmarried daughter included. Because the daughter is close to 21, the family files immediately and an attorney verifies her CSPA protection.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — What if my spouse was a green card holder, not a U.S. citizen?

Then this route is not yours: the widow(er) Form I-360 self-petition is for spouses of U.S. citizens only. If your spouse was a green-card holder who had already filed an I-130 for you, different and narrower doors may exist — for example, relief under INA §204(l) for certain surviving relatives, or humanitarian reinstatement of an approved petition. Those are legal arguments, not simple paperwork, and they have their own conditions and deadlines. Legal help is strongly recommended for this route — a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit is the safest door, and a document preparer can support the clerical packet alongside them. The choice is still yours: DIY ($25 per form), a preparer (clerical only), an attorney, or a DOJ nonprofit.

Example: a husband with a green card filed an I-130 for his wife, then died. The wife cannot use the widow(er) I-360 — an attorney reviews her case for §204(l) relief or reinstatement instead.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 (U.S. citizen spouses) — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — What if I remarry?

Plainly: remarrying before your widow(er) case is approved can end your eligibility. The widow(er) route requires that you have not remarried. Do not remarry until your green card is in your hand — and if wedding plans exist, talk to an attorney before the wedding, not after, because the order of events decides the case.

Example: a widow is engaged 18 months after her husband's death, with her I-360 still pending. She waits, on her attorney's advice, until her green card is approved before the wedding.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

Widow / widower — Where do I get help? Your four choices

A widow(er) case carries a hard 2-year deadline, a bona-fide-marriage evidence record, and — for many families — children close to 21. These cases involve legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended — an attorney's legal review protects you, the preparer, and the case. But the choice is yours: (1) DIY — file it yourself, $25 per form, with the checklist + teach guide; (2) Document Preparer — clerical preparation only, no legal advice (Form I-360: Basic $599 / Standard $750 / Premium $900); (3) Licensed Attorney; or (4) DOJ Nonprofit. If you choose DIY or a preparer, we strongly recommend you also get an attorney to review it — Review $99 per form, Human Review $199. You can also text us at (772) 971-6129 for a free 15-minute call and we will help you find one.

Urgent Help

Something is happening now. First: breathe. Second: find the date. Almost every immigration emergency is a deadline problem, and deadlines are handled in order.

A family member was detained

Do not sign anything you do not understand. Read Detained now, then call an attorney or DOJ nonprofit.

A letter has a deadline under 30 days

Decode it with the Mail Scanner. If it is an RFE, use the RFE Decoder. If it is a Notice of Intent to Deny, that is a legal fight — attorney first.

You got a denial

Read If Denied? — appeal and motion deadlines are short and unforgiving.

You have a court date (NTA)

Read Immigration Court. Never miss a hearing — a missed hearing can mean a removal order.

Someone is hurting you at home

If you are in danger now, call 911. National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 (TTY 1-800-787-3224), text “START” to 88788 — free, confidential, 24/7. And read this: if the abuser is your U.S. citizen or green card holder spouse, parent, or adult child, you may be able to get a green card on your own, without them ever knowing — Domestic Violence — VAWA Green Card. Victim of a crime or trafficking? See the U Visa & T Visa page.

We are not a law firm. In a true emergency, an attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit is the right first call — find one on the EOIR roster — by state (PDF) ↗, EOIR R&A Roster reports page ↗, EOIR Recognition & Accreditation Program page ↗.

Detained — a family member was taken

Read this first, before you sign or pay anything.

The three rules

  1. Do not sign anything you do not understand — including “voluntary” departure papers. Ask for an interpreter and for a lawyer.
  2. Get the A-number and the facility. Use ICE's Online Detainee Locator (locator.ice.gov) with the A-number and country of birth, or name and date of birth.
  3. Call an immigration attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit the same day. Detention cases move fast, and bond and hearing deadlines are legal questions a preparer cannot handle.

Check court dates on the EOIR automated hotline: 1-800-898-7180 (enter the A-number). Keep a written log of every call: date, time, who you spoke to.

Open the official EOIR roster — by state (PDF) ↗ Open the EOIR R&A Roster reports page ↗ Open the EOIR Recognition & Accreditation Program page ↗

If the detained person was also being abused by a U.S. citizen or green card holder spouse, parent, or adult child — or was the victim of a crime or trafficking — tell the attorney on day one: VAWA and the U visa / T visa can protect victims even in hard cases, and they are confidential.

Prepare the family with the Emergency Family Readiness Vault checklist — before an emergency, not during one.

If Denied?

A denial letter is not the end of the road — but the road from here is legal, time-limited, and unforgiving about deadlines. Read the letter before you do anything else.

First moves

  1. Find the deadline in the denial letter — appeals and motions (Form I-290B) usually must be filed within about 30 days.
  2. Have an immigration attorney review the denial before you file anything — the right move (appeal, motion to reopen, motion to reconsider, or a fresh filing) depends on why USCIS denied it.
  3. Do not simply re-file the same packet — if the reason was legal, a new filing gets the same answer.

I-290B is in the form directory (Basic $599 / Standard $750 / Premium $899) — but the brief or statement of errors is legal writing, and we strongly recommend an attorney for it.

Immigration Court

Removal proceedings (a Notice to Appear) are a court case against the government. There is no preparer checkout on this page, because no preparer may stand beside you in court.

What you must know

  • Never miss a hearing. Missing one can produce a removal order without you there.
  • Check your date any time: EOIR hotline 1-800-898-7180 with the A-number — court dates and addresses change.
  • There is no free lawyer provided in immigration court, but free legal-service providers exist — the court hands out a list; the EOIR roster lists recognized organizations.
  • Keep your address current with the court (Form EOIR-33) — hearing notices are mailed.

Open the official EOIR roster — by state (PDF) ↗ Open the EOIR R&A Roster reports page ↗ Open the EOIR Recognition & Accreditation Program page ↗

Scam Shield

Immigration fear is a business model for scammers. These are the traps we see — and the checks that defeat them.

Red flags

  • “Notario” offering legal help — in the U.S., a notary is not a lawyer
  • Anyone who guarantees approval, a visa, or a work permit
  • Demands for gift cards, wire transfers, or crypto — USCIS never asks for these
  • Charging for blank USCIS forms — forms are free at uscis.gov
  • “USCIS” calling from a number that asks for payment by phone
  • Keeping your original documents hostage until you pay more

The checks that defeat them

  • Attorneys: verify the state bar number
  • Nonprofits: verify them on the official EOIR roster
  • Fees: confirm the current government fee at uscis.gov/fees yourself
  • Always get a written agreement and a copy of everything filed
  • Never sign a form you have not read, in a language you understand

Trust & Compliance — our rules

Guide: 4 Basic Rules to a Green Card

What every applicant must pass — explained the way we explain it across the kitchen table.

1 · An eligible pathway

Someone must sponsor you — a qualifying U.S. citizen or green-card holder relative, an employer, or a humanitarian category you qualify for.

2 · A visa must be available

Immediate relatives of U.S. citizens always have one. Preference categories wait for the Visa Bulletin — see the Priority Date Monitor.

3 · Lawful entry or an exception

Adjustment inside the U.S. generally needs an inspected entry (visa, border card, parole, I-94). Exceptions exist — 245(i), waivers, humanitarian relief — and they are lawyer territory.

4 · Admissibility and money

No bars that apply to you (or a waiver that covers them), and a sponsor who meets the 2026 income line — household of 4 at 125%: $41,250 — see the Sponsor Qualifier.

Guide: Filing Forms Properly

Four habits that prevent automatic rejections.

Use the exact current edition & fee

USCIS rejects packets immediately if a form edition is outdated or the payment is off — I-485 takes only the 09/18/26 edition. Confirm both on the form's uscis.gov page the week you mail.

Sign everything, in black ink, by hand where required

An unsigned form is a rejected packet.

Answer every question

Write “N/A” or “None” where the instructions allow — blank fields can trigger the PA-2026-05 rule that lets USCIS deny an incomplete packet without an RFE.

Translate and copy completely

Every foreign-language document needs a full certified English translation, and every copy must show the whole document, all four corners.

Run the Packet X-Ray before you mail

Guide: After Getting a Green Card

Becoming a resident is not the finish line. Three rules keep the card safe.

Conditional 2-year cards must be renewed on time

If you were married less than 2 years when the card was granted, file I-751 during the 90 days before it expires — see the Renewal Alerts calculator.

Residence is real, not just a card

Long trips abroad can be treated as abandoning your residence. Keep trips under 6 months where you can, and get advice before any trip near a year.

Keep your record clean and current

File AR-11 within 10 days of moving, file taxes as a resident, and keep proof — your future I-751 and N-400 depend on this paper trail.

My Family Abroad — Their Own Login, Checklist, Language & Case Watch

Their own login

The family-abroad checklist — try it

This is the checklist your family member works through in their own login. Tap an item when it is done — this demo works on this page only and saves nothing.

✓Valid passport — valid for at least 6 months beyond the planned entry date.
✓Birth certificate — long-form, plus a full certified English translation if it is not in English.
✓Marriage certificate — if married (and proof every earlier marriage ended, if any).
✓Police clearance certificate(s) — from your country of residence and any country where you lived 12 months or more since age 16, as NVC requires.
✓Civil documents uploaded to CEAC — scanned clearly, one document per file, in the order NVC lists them.

After You Become a Citizen — What Comes Next

The oath ceremony is not the end of your family's story — it is the start of the next chapter, and NIPTEI stays with you for it. The client who becomes a citizen can do things a green card holder cannot: bring parents right away, sponsor family in faster lanes, vote, and hold a U.S. passport. Here is the whole page, in plain English.

First, the road here — Form N-400

Most green card holders apply after 5 years — or 3 years if married to and living with a U.S. citizen spouse. Prepare with N-400 Test Prep and Civics Practice, and see what the day looks like on the Oath Ceremony page. USCIS fee is separate from any help you choose — see the N-400 on the Choose a Form page.

Bring your parents

A U.S. citizen age 21 or older can file Form I-130 for a parent as an immediate relative — no yearly waiting line for a visa number. Step by step: Family Filing Guides — filing for a parent.

Bring your spouse or children

Your spouse and your unmarried children under 21 are also immediate relatives of a U.S. citizen. Married children and siblings of citizens file in the family preference categories — the route, the documents, and the honest wait are in the Family Filing Guides. Check your income first with the Sponsor Qualifier — locked to 2026.

Register to vote

Once you have taken the oath, you may register to vote in your state and vote in U.S. elections — one of the real rights of citizenship. Register with your state's election office or at a government office when you update your ID. Never register or vote before you are a citizen — claiming to be a citizen to vote can destroy an immigration case. If you are not sure, ask first.

Get a U.S. passport

Apply in person at a passport acceptance facility (many post offices and libraries) with Form DS-11, your Certificate of Naturalization (bring the original — it is returned to you), your state ID, a passport photo, and the State Department fee. A U.S. passport book is also the strongest everyday proof of citizenship — most new citizens apply right after the oath.

Keep the family's cases in one place

The petitions you file next live in the same hub as the case that made you a citizen — checklist, tracker, renewal alerts, and documents in My Immigration, In One Place. And if your family member is still abroad, they follow along in My Family Abroad.

Read the Family Filing Guides Sponsor Qualifier (2026) N-400 Test Prep Life After the Green Card

Emergency Family Readiness Vault — one-tap crisis plan

If a parent is detained or hospitalized, the children still need school pickup, medicine, and a calm adult with authority to act. Build this packet before an emergency.

The readiness checklist

  • Emergency contacts — family, school, doctor, attorney / DOJ nonprofit
  • Caregiver authorization for the children, signed and notarized where your state allows
  • Copies of IDs, birth certificates, and immigration documents for every family member, in one folder a trusted person can reach
  • Medicines, allergies, and doctor information for each child
  • School pickup authorizations on file with the school
  • The EOIR hotline (1-800-898-7180) and the ICE detainee locator written on paper, not only in a phone

On this static page nothing is stored in a vault — keep the paper folder with your trusted person. Encrypted vault storage comes with the live back-end. A caregiver authorization is a legal document; a DOJ nonprofit or attorney in your state can confirm the right form.

What counts as proof (marriage cases)

Document Vault — templates, photo guide & secure intake

The paper tools that prevent rejections: the translation rules, the 2×2 photo rules, and how secure intake works in the live system.

🔒 Your documents are safe

Your documents are encrypted. Only you and your assigned professional (and the founder) can see them. They are never public, never sold, and you can delete them anytime. Every time someone opens one of your documents, it is written in the audit log — who, when, and what document.

Certified translation rules

Every foreign-language document needs a full, exact English translation, plus the translator's signed certificate of competence and accuracy. Machine printouts without the certificate get RFEs. The translator cannot be you or your spouse for your own case.

Passport photo rules (2×2)

2×2 inches, color, white background, taken within 6 months, full face facing the camera, no glasses, no filters, no photocopies of photos. Most I-485 / I-765 packets need 2.

Who can see your documents — the lockdown rule

Only you, your assigned professional, and the founder. No one else — not another client, not another preparer, and not a law student who is not assigned to your case. In production, Supabase row-level security enforces this: an unassigned account gets zero of your documents.

N-400 Test Prep — Citizenship

Most green-card holders can apply after 5 years as a resident — or 3 years if married to and living with the same U.S. citizen spouse the whole time. The interview tests English and civics, and USCIS reviews your whole record.

The test

English: read one sentence, write one sentence, and speak English during the interview itself. Civics: study the version that applies to your filing date (2008 vs 2025 test). Practice with the Civics Practice flashcards.

Good Moral Character — Nov 4, 2026 policy (PM-602-0201)

USCIS now looks closely at tax compliance, child support (even without a court order), compliance with an I-864 support obligation you signed, and public-benefits history. Bring tax transcripts (5 years, or 3 if married to a U.S. citizen), child-support proof if it applies, and I-864 compliance proof if you were sponsored. Our N-400 tiers: $199 / $400 / $600 — see Choose a Form.

Family Sponsorship Multiplier — the multi-generation roadmap

Families rarely bring just one person. Map everyone you hope to reunite with, and see the fastest legal sequence — because one person's new status can open the next person's door.

The classic sequence

  1. A green-card holder naturalizes (N-400) — and can now petition for parents, married children, and siblings, which a green-card holder cannot.
  2. Parents of a U.S. citizen are immediate relatives — no quota wait.
  3. A spouse who arrives as a resident can later petition in F2A/F2B for their own relatives.
  4. Each approval starts that person's own citizenship countdown.

Run each person's route in the Path Finder — and remember its limit: a green-card holder cannot petition for a parent, a married child, or a brother or sister.

15 Things To Know Before Anyone Files For You

Fifteen topics families get surprised by — gathered in one place, in plain English, each with the official source and a real example. Read the ones that touch your case before you pay anyone, sign anything, travel anywhere, or miss a deadline.

General information, not legal advice. Every section below explains published government rules and names its source. NIPTEI is a document preparation service, not a law firm. Where a section says "get an attorney," it means it: a licensed immigration attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit is the right next step, not a form. No one can guarantee that a petition or visa will be approved.

1 · Scam Shield — how to spot an immigration scam

No one from USCIS will call you and demand money by gift card, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency — ever. USCIS contacts you by paper mail and through your official online account; it does not threaten arrest by phone or sell faster processing. Three rules catch almost every scam: no one can guarantee approval — anyone who does is lying; no one can "speed up" your case for a fee — there is no such product; and never pay for a blank form — every USCIS form is free at uscis.gov. A real USCIS notice is a paper letter (or an official account message) with your receipt number, the form name, and dates — not a text demanding payment today.

Example: A caller says your case will be deported unless you buy $800 of gift cards in the next hour. That is a scam, word for word. Hang up, keep your receipt notices, and check your real status in the Case Tracker.

Report a scam: USCIS (report immigration scams from the USCIS website), the Federal Trade Commission at ftc.gov ↗, and your state attorney general. Full page: Scam Shield. · General information, not legal advice.

2 · Detained or in immigration court — the first 24 hours

If someone is detained: do not sign a stipulated removal or "voluntary departure" paper you do not understand — signing can waive the hearing. The person has the right to a hearing before an immigration judge and the right to a lawyer — at their own expense; the government does not provide one. Find them through ICE's Online Detainee Locator, and check the court date on the EOIR hotline: 1-800-898-7180 with the A-number. Missing a hearing can produce a removal order without them there. A document preparer cannot represent anyone in court — only a licensed attorney or a DOJ-accredited representative can.

Example: A father is picked up on Friday. His family spends the weekend calling a preparer. The correct weekend moves are: locate him, get the A-number, check the EOIR hotline, and get an attorney or DOJ nonprofit on the case before any paper is signed.

Full pages: Detained · Immigration Court · EOIR hotline 1-800-898-7180. Source: uscis.gov ↗ and the EOIR roster at justice.gov. · General information, not legal advice.

3 · Travel warning — do not leave the U.S. without checking first

Leaving the United States at the wrong moment can cancel a pending case (an I-485 is generally treated as abandoned if you leave without Advance Parole), can trigger the 3-year or 10-year unlawful-presence bars when someone who accrued unlawful presence departs, and can end with being refused re-entry — the risk is highest for anyone who entered without inspection, overstayed, or has any pending application. Advance Parole (Form I-131) is permission to ask to return — it is not a promise you will be let back in. A parole decision is made by the officer when you land.

Example: An applicant with a pending I-485 flies home for a funeral without Advance Parole. The I-485 is treated as abandoned — the emergency was real, and the rule applied anyway.

Full page: Travel Safety Check. Source: INA §212(a)(9)(B) and USCIS travel guidance — uscis.gov ↗. · General information, not legal advice. If anyone in the case has unlawful presence or a prior removal: attorney first, plane ticket second.

4 · If you are denied — what happens next

Learn four words apart. A rejection means USCIS never accepted the filing (wrong fee, wrong edition, missing signature) — no case exists; you fix and refile. A denial means USCIS decided the case against you — the denial notice says why and what you may do. An RFE asks for more evidence by a deadline; a NOID says USCIS intends to deny and gives you one chance to answer — both deadlines are short and do not move. After a denial, options may include an appeal or motion on Form I-290B (generally due within 30 days of the decision — the notice controls), refiling if facts or law allow, or doing nothing — and choosing wrong wastes the deadline. That choice is legal work.

Example: A denial arrives with a 30-day I-290B window. The family waits three weeks, then looks for help. Read the notice the day it comes, count the days, and see an attorney in week one.

Full page: If Denied? · Form I-290B — uscis.gov/i-290b ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

5 · Address changes — AR-11 and the 10-day rule

Most noncitizens must tell USCIS about a move within 10 days, on Form AR-11 — for every pending case. USCIS mails biometrics appointments, interview notices, and decisions to the address it has; a notice sent to your old address still counts, and a missed interview can end the case. A sponsor has the same duty on Form I-865 within 30 days, for as long as the I-864 obligation lasts. A family member abroad in consular processing updates their address through the NVC / CEAC case, so the interview letter reaches them.

Example: A couple moves in March and files AR-11 in June "when things settle." The April interview notice went to the old apartment. The case is denied for failure to appear — the move was legal; the silence was the problem.

Full page: AR-11 Helper · Form AR-11 — uscis.gov/ar-11 ↗ · Sponsor address: Form I-865 — uscis.gov/i-865 ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

6 · Work, travel, and life while you wait

While an I-485 is pending, work is allowed only with a valid Employment Authorization Document (Form I-765) — filing the green-card case by itself is not work permission. Travel follows section 3 above: Advance Parole or stay put. Renew the EAD 180 days before it expires — because as of October 14, 2026, USCIS ended the automatic extension of work permits for late renewals (Federal Register Doc. 2026-20955): if your card expires and the renewal is still pending, you may have to stop working until the new card arrives. That is the single most expensive calendar mistake of 2026.

Example: A nurse renews her EAD 30 days before expiry, counting on the old automatic extension. There isn't one anymore. Her employer must take her off the schedule when the card lapses.

Source: Federal Register Doc. 2026-20955, explained in News & Deadlines — federalregister.gov ↗ · Renewal dates: Renewal Alerts. · General information, not legal advice.

7 · Life after the green card

A marriage-based green card approved before the 2nd wedding anniversary is conditional for 2 years: file Form I-751 jointly in the 90 days before it expires (the window opens at 21 months) to remove the conditions — missing that window puts the resident out of status. Citizenship comes later: Form N-400 at 3 years if married to and living with a U.S. citizen, otherwise 5 years — and long trips abroad can break continuous residence (a trip over 6 months can raise a presumption you abandoned residence; over 1 year generally breaks it). A lost, stolen, or expired card is replaced with Form I-90 — an expired card does not end your status, but it can end your ability to prove it at a job or a border.

Example: A conditional resident calendars the I-751 for "the month the card expires." The joint window closes 90 days of paperwork earlier than her reminder — she files at month 21, inside the window, instead.

Full pages: Life After the Green Card · After Getting a Green Card · I-751 USCIS fee is $750 paper filing. Source: uscis.gov ↗. · General information, not legal advice.

8 · Taxes, child support, and Good Moral Character for citizenship

Naturalization requires Good Moral Character for the statutory period — 5 years for most applicants, 3 for spouses of U.S. citizens — and USCIS's November 4, 2026 policy memorandum PM-602-0201 put everyday money conduct at the center of that judgment. What it means in practice: bring tax transcripts for the full period (5 years for most N-400 applicants); unfiled returns or an unpaid tax debt with no payment arrangement count against you. Child support counts even without a court order — willfully failing to support your children is a Good Moral Character problem whether or not a judge ever signed an order. I-864 compliance counts — a sponsor who ignored their affidavit-of-support duty carries that into the GMC analysis. And public-benefits use is weighed in context, under the same memo's framework — read the full explanation in News before you assume any single fact decides your case.

Example: A father applies for citizenship owing two years of support he agreed to pay informally. No court order exists. Under PM-602-0201, USCIS can still treat the unpaid support as a Good Moral Character failure. He pays, documents it, and files with an attorney's review.

This section has its own full treatment on What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone (§§3–4) and in News & Deadlines (the November 4, 2026 memo). Source: USCIS Policy Memorandum PM-602-0201 — uscis.gov ↗. · General information, not legal advice.

9 · Sponsor dies, divorces, or loses their job

Three different events, three different rules. Death of the sponsor: the I-864 support duty ends when the sponsor dies — but the case may not have to die with them: USCIS can allow a substitute sponsor (a qualifying close relative) when a petitioner dies after the petition is approved, under humanitarian reinstatement rules. Ask an attorney before assuming either way. Divorce: divorce does not end the I-864 duty — a sponsor who divorces the immigrant still owes it. But divorce before the green card is granted can end a marriage-based case itself, because the qualifying relationship is gone. Job loss: the I-864 is judged on current income when USCIS decides — a sponsor who loses a job can add countable assets (3× / 5× the shortfall) or bring in a joint sponsor who qualifies on their own household.

Example: A petitioner dies two months after the I-130 is approved. The family assumes the case is over. With an attorney, the widow asks USCIS for humanitarian reinstatement and a substitute sponsor — her brother-in-law, a U.S. citizen who meets the income line, signs a new I-864.

Sources: USCIS Form I-864 instructions and humanitarian reinstatement guidance — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗ · Sponsor Qualifier. · General information, not legal advice — death and divorce cases go to an attorney first.

10 · Children turning 21 — the Child Status Protection Act (CSPA)

A "child" in immigration law is generally unmarried and under 21 — and cases can take years, so Congress passed the Child Status Protection Act to freeze some children's ages. In plain English: for many family cases, the child's CSPA age is their age when a visa becomes available minus the time the petition was pending — and the child must then seek to acquire the green card (file the I-485 or DS-260) within 1 year of availability, or the protection is lost. Immediate relatives of U.S. citizens keep the age they were when the I-130 was filed. Preference-category children (of green-card holders, and married/divorced children) are where aging out really happens.

Example: A daughter is 20 when her father's I-130 is filed and 22 when her priority date becomes current — but the petition was pending 2 years, so her CSPA age is 20. She files her I-485 within the year and is treated as a child. Wait 13 months instead, and the protection is gone.

Source: USCIS, Child Status Protection Act — uscis.gov — Child Status Protection Act (CSPA) ↗. If a child in your case turns 21 within a year, do not wait — attorney, now. · General information, not legal advice.

11 · Priority Dates and the Visa Bulletin, in plain English

Your Priority Date is the day USCIS received your petition — your place in line. Family categories beyond immediate relatives have yearly quotas, so the State Department publishes a monthly Visa Bulletin with two charts: Final Action Dates (whose cases can be finished now) and Dates for Filing (whose cases can be started now, when USCIS announces the filing chart applies). Your case can move when your Priority Date is earlier than the date printed for your category and country. Some categories and countries — siblings of U.S. citizens, and applicants from Mexico, India, China, and the Philippines — wait many years because demand exceeds the quota, not because anything is wrong with the case.

Example: A brother's Priority Date is March 3, 2020, in the F4 sibling category. The Bulletin's F4 Final Action Date reads February 1, 2020. His date is later than the printed date — not yet. When the chart passes March 3, 2020, his case can finish.

Full page: Priority Date Monitor. Source: U.S. Department of State, Visa Bulletin — travel.state.gov — Visa Bulletin ↗. · General information, not legal advice.

12 · Processing times — how to read them, and when to ask

USCIS publishes a processing-time range for each form and office: the range shows how long most cases like yours took — the top of the range is not a promise and the bottom is not a delay. A case is officially "outside normal processing time" only when it passes the date USCIS posts for that form and office — and that is when you can file an e-Request ("case inquiry") asking USCIS to look. Before that date, inquiries are answered with the same range. Longer routes exist for true emergencies and errors (expedite requests, the USCIS Contact Center, your congressional office's immigration liaison) — but a case inside its posted range is a case that is simply in line, however hard that is to hear.

Example: Your I-485 shows a posted range of 12–18 months at your office and you are at month 10 with a receipt notice and completed biometrics. Nothing is wrong, and an e-Request will say so. At month 19 with no movement, file the e-Request the week the case goes outside the range.

Source: USCIS "Check Case Processing Times" and e-Request tools — uscis.gov ↗ · Case Tracker. · General information, not legal advice.

13 · Biometrics, interview, and medical exam — what actually happens on the day

Biometrics is a short appointment at an Application Support Center: photo, fingerprints, signature — bring the appointment notice and a government photo ID. It is a background-check step, not a test. The medical exam is done by a USCIS civil surgeon (inside the U.S.) or a panel physician (abroad): a physical exam, vaccination review, and the sealed Form I-693 — do not open the sealed envelope; an opened envelope must be redone. The interview is a sworn conversation with an officer: bring every original of every document you copied, your ID, and — for marriage cases — both spouses and your bona-fide-marriage evidence. The officer verifies identity, eligibility, and truthfulness. Miss any of the three without rescheduling and the case can be denied as abandoned.

Example: A husband opens the sealed medical envelope at home "to check it." At the interview, the officer cannot accept an opened I-693 — new exam, new fee to the doctor, new delay. The envelope stays sealed until an officer or the surgeon's process opens it.

Full pages: Interview Day · Interview Preparation. Source: USCIS form instructions — uscis.gov ↗. · General information, not legal advice.

14 · State-by-state rules for preparers — read yours before you pay

Federal law says who may give legal advice; state law separately regulates paid non-attorney preparers, and the rules differ by state. Two examples every client should know: California's Immigration Consultant Act requires immigration consultants to register with the Secretary of State, post a surety bond, use a written contract with required disclosures, and never call themselves attorneys or "notarios" with legal authority. New York's Immigrant Assistance Service Provider law requires a written contract in the client's language, itemized fees, posted notices of what the provider may and may not do, and a 72-hour right to cancel the contract. Other states have their own versions — and some have none of these specific statutes. USCIS does not publish a single national preparer rule — do not assume your state works like another state.

Example: A New York client signs a preparer contract on Monday and thinks better of it on Wednesday. New York's 72-hour cancellation right is exactly for her — if she lived under a different state's rules, that right might not exist in the same form.

These summaries are general information for orientation only — they are drafts for a licensed attorney in your state to review before they are relied on live. Your preparer must show you your own state's rules before payment. Source: California Business & Professions Code (Immigration Consultant Act) and New York General Business Law (Immigrant Assistance Services) — check your state legislature's website. · General information, not legal advice.

15 · The "Do Not File" list — when NIPTEI will not file for you

This platform exists to file — and there are cases we will not file, because filing them as clerical packets would hurt the client. NIPTEI will not file: a case for someone who entered without inspection with no lawful pathway mapped by an attorney; a case with a prior removal or deportation and no waiver strategy; any case built on fraud or false documents — ever, for anyone; and any case whose real question is legal — waivers, asylum strategy, court, criminal-history analysis — where we strongly recommend a lawyer goes first. And the choice of help is always yours — DIY ($25 per form, with the checklist + teach guide), a document preparer (clerical preparation only, no legal advice), a licensed attorney, or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit; if you choose DIY or a preparer on a case like this, we strongly recommend an attorney review too (Review $99 per form, Human Review $199). What NIPTEI will never do is file a case built on fraud or false documents. "Will not file" is never a dead end here: every one of these routes to a licensed immigration attorney or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit, with your documents and your story organized for them — and many return to file with us, with the attorney, once the legal path is clear.

Example: A young man with a prior removal order asks us to "just file the I-130." We do not take his money. We send him — packet organized, history written down — to an attorney to evaluate an I-212 and waiver route first. If that route opens, we prepare the clerical packet with the attorney. If it doesn't, he learned it before USCIS did.

Start here: Do Not File Danger Shield · Before You File — Know Everything In Advance. · General information, not legal advice.

I was the victim of a crime — is there a visa for me? Possibly the U visa (Form I-918): qualifying crime + substantial harm + helping law enforcement. See the U Visa & T Visa page.
