Before You File — Know Everything In Advance

Know In Advance — All In One Place, So You Will Not Be Surprised. This page is written for the two people about to start a case together: the document preparer or attorney who will file the form, and the client whose name goes on it. Everything you are agreeing to — the forms, the money, the documents, the time, the risks, who does what, and what happens after filing — is on this one page, in plain English, before anyone pays or signs anything.

General information, not legal advice. This page explains how filing works and what this platform charges. It is not legal advice for any specific case. Preparers on this platform are non-attorney document preparers — clerical help only. Cases with legal questions go to a licensed immigration attorney or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit. No one can guarantee that a petition or visa will be approved.
Honest status on this public page: saved accounts, live SMS/email, live Stripe payments, and live USCIS case lookup do NOT work on this static page — they come with the live back-end. Nothing here files, charges, or sends anything by itself.

1 · Before you start — the forms, the order, and the editions

Using the most common route on this platform — a spouse's green card through adjustment of status — the packet is built in this order, and most of it is filed together, in one packet, when the applicant is eligible to file concurrently:

  • Form I-130 (Petition for Alien Relative) with Form I-130A for a spouse — I-130A is never filed alone; it travels with the I-130 at no extra charge.
  • Form I-485 (Adjustment of Status) — filed with the I-130 when concurrent filing is allowed; if the relative is outside the U.S., the I-130 goes first alone, and the rest happens later at the National Visa Center (see the NVC & Department of State guide).
  • Form I-864 (Affidavit of Support) — filed with the I-485 (or at the NVC stage for consular cases). It is not an opening move by itself: it supports a green-card application, it does not start one.
  • Form I-765 (work permit) and Form I-131 (travel permit) — optional, filed with or after the I-485.
  • Form I-693 — the medical exam, completed by a USCIS civil surgeon and submitted sealed.
  • Form I-751 comes much later and stands on its own clock: filed jointly in the 90 days before a 2-year conditional green card expires.

Mandatory editions — no exceptions. The I-485 edition dated 09/18/26 and the I-864 edition dated 08/24/26 are the only editions USCIS accepts. File on an older edition and USCIS rejects the packet: it is returned unfiled, no receipt number is issued, and no filing date is protected. Edition dates are printed at the bottom of every form — the Packet Health Check verifies every one before mailing.

Example: A couple mails a perfect packet on the old I-485 edition. Three weeks later the whole packet comes back with a rejection notice. They refile on the 09/18/26 edition — and their case starts the day the second packet is accepted, not the first. If we prepared that packet and used the wrong edition, our completeness promise applies: we fix it free.

Source: USCIS form pages and edition dates — uscis.gov/i-485 ↗ · uscis.gov/i-864 ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

Basic — we type the form from your exact answers, check the form edition and blank fields, and give filing instructions.
Standard — Basic, plus your evidence checklist: we tell you every document needed, gather and check them with you, and assemble the packet with a cover letter.
Premium — Standard, plus Human Review, the Packet Health Check, priority handling, RFE / notice follow-up help, and we submit all of the documents for you.

Marriage & Family Green Card Bundle: Basic $999 · Standard $1,799 · Premium $2,799 (you save $528 / $649 / $451 versus one-by-one). Single-form tier prices are on Choose a Form. Form I-730 is a single flat $299 preparer fee — no tiers.

USCIS Government Fees — paid to USCIS

I-485 (paper filing): $1,440
I-130: $675
I-751 (paper filing): $750
I-730: $0

Confirm every government fee on Form G-1055 at uscis.gov on filing day — USCIS rejects packets sent with an old fee. These totals are never added to the service-fee column.

How you pay the service fee — your choice, nothing pre-selected: Pay in Full (full amount now, one payment, no extra fee), Pay in 3 (3 equal payments, no extra fee — bundle: $333.00 × 3 / $599.67 × 3 / $933.00 × 3), or the Monthly Payment Plan (scheduled monthly payments via Stripe — 6 or 12 months, first payment today, the rest auto-charged monthly by Stripe, total stays the same, no extra fee — bundle: $166.50/mo or $83.25/mo · $299.83/mo or $149.92/mo · $466.50/mo or $233.25/mo). If you choose Pay in 3 or Monthly, you review and sign an Installment Contract before paying — it states your total, the amounts and due dates, that USCIS fees are separate and not part of the installments, that work starts on the first payment, and that filing happens only after all payments are received. The contract is a draft template for a licensed attorney to review before live use, and the checkout shows it in full. Payments are processed securely by Stripe. Live Stripe checkout is connected in production — on this static page the payment choice is saved with your order and a Stripe payment link / invoice is sent to you.

⚠ MISSED-PAYMENT RULE — stated plainly, not in small print: If you miss a payment, 50% is added to the total amount.
Example: on a $999 total, a missed payment adds $499.50, making the total $1,498.50. The rule for any total: missed payment = total × 50% added.

USCIS fees are different money. They are paid to USCIS — in our packets, electronically with Form G-1450 (card) or Form G-1650 (ACH) only, no paper checks. And USCIS states that its fees are non-refundable regardless of the decision: a denied case does not get its government fees back. That is all USCIS says — we do not add to it.

Sources: USCIS fee schedule, Form G-1055 — uscis.gov/g-1055 ↗ · Form G-1450 — uscis.gov/g-1450 ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

3 · All the documents, up front

For the spouse route, the full evidence checklist is built before anyone pays — and it is the same list the Packet Workspace works from: marriage certificate and proof the marriage is real (joint lease, bank accounts, tax returns, insurance, photos over time); divorce or death certificates ending every prior marriage; birth certificates and government IDs; passport-style photos; the sponsor's IRS tax transcripts, 6 months of pay stubs, and an employment letter; and the sealed Form I-693 medical exam — the envelope must arrive sealed; an opened envelope does not count.

  • Translations: every document not in English needs a full English translation with a signed Certificate of Accuracy — the translator certifies they are competent and the translation is complete and accurate (8 CFR 103.2(b)(3)). A summary, a machine printout without certification, or a translation by the applicant themselves does not meet the rule.
  • Credit freeze: if the sponsor has a credit freeze, it must be lifted at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion before filing — USCIS and background-check systems cannot verify what they cannot see, and a frozen file stalls the case.
  • What does not count: uncertified translations, an opened medical envelope, expired form editions, and unsigned forms. Each one is a rejection or a delay that did not have to happen.

Example: A birth certificate arrives with a careful translation — but no signed Certificate of Accuracy. Under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(3) that translation is incomplete evidence. The fix costs a signature before filing; after filing, it can cost an RFE and months.

Source: 8 CFR 103.2(b)(3) (translations) and USCIS form instructions — uscis.gov ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

4 · All the time, up front

  • Our preparation time (after all your documents are received — the clock never starts before): Standard 5–7 business days · Rush 2–3 business days · 24-Hour Express within 24 hours.
  • USCIS processing time is set by USCIS, varies by form and office, and changes — USCIS publishes its own processing times, and we will show you the range USCIS publishes for your form rather than promise you a date nobody can promise.
  • Biometrics: after filing, USCIS schedules a fingerprint appointment at an Application Support Center — usually early in the case. Miss it without rescheduling and the case can be treated as abandoned.
  • Interview: most family green-card cases end with an in-person interview. Both spouses attend a marriage case interview together.
  • Outside the U.S.: after the I-130 is approved, the case moves to the National Visa Center: fees, the DS-260, document upload in CEAC, "Documentarily Qualified," then the embassy interview — explained step by step in the NVC & Department of State guide.
  • Renewal windows to write down now: I-751 — file at 21 months (the 90 days before a 2-year card expires); N-400 — citizenship at 3 years (married to a U.S. citizen) or 5 years; EAD work permit — renew 180 days before it expires.
  • Delays and RFEs: a Request for Evidence pauses your case until you answer, and the answer deadline printed on the RFE does not move. A clean, complete packet is the only real speed-up there is.

Example: A packet filed in January draws an RFE in April asking for the sponsor's tax transcript. The family answers in the last week of the deadline instead of the first — the case resumes months later than it needed to. The RFE did not slow the case; the wait to answer it did.

Source: USCIS processing-times and form instructions — uscis.gov ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

5 · All the risks, up front

Know these before you file, not after:

  • Incomplete packets can be denied without a warning letter. Under USCIS policy memorandum PA-2026-05, an application filed without the required initial evidence can be denied outright — without an RFE or a Notice of Intent to Deny first. "File it and see what they ask for" is not a strategy anymore.
  • The clerical killers: wrong fee, wrong form edition, missing signature, missing or uncertified translation. Every one is preventable before mailing — and none is fixable after a denial.
  • Red-flag history changes everything: entered without inspection, overstay, a prior removal or deportation, an arrest or conviction, a prior denial, or a prior marriage USCIS questioned. Any of these can turn a routine filing into a legal case — or make filing itself dangerous.

What to do: pause and read the warning first. These cases involve legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended — a licensed immigration attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit is the safest first step, and an attorney's legal review protects you, the preparer, and the case. But the choice is yours: you may file alone (DIY, $25 per form), use a document preparer (clerical preparation only, no legal advice), or get an attorney or DOJ representative — and if you choose DIY or a preparer, we strongly recommend an attorney review as well (Review $99 per form, Human Review $199). Run the Do Not File Danger Shield before any of these cases, and read What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone for what the I-864 contract and your debts really mean.

Example: A man who entered without inspection and later married a U.S. citizen files an I-485 on his own. Adjustment is not open to him on these facts, and the filing puts him on the government's desk instead of on a path. An attorney first would have mapped the consular-and-waiver route — or told him not to file at all yet.

Source: USCIS policy guidance including PA-2026-05, explained in News & Deadlines — uscis.gov ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

6 · Who does what, up front

Document Preparer — clerical only

Types your exact answers at your direction, tells you every document needed, gathers and checks them with you, assembles and submits the packet. A preparer gives no legal advice and makes no eligibility decision — the choice of form is yours, confirmed by the User Direction agreement you sign.

Attorney / DOJ Representative — legal help

Gives legal advice, decides strategy, handles waivers, court, and red-flag cases, and represents you before USCIS — recorded on Form G-28. DOJ-accredited representatives do the same within their organization's recognition, often free or sliding-scale.

You, the Client — the decisions and the truth

You choose the form (User Direction), you review every page before it is mailed, and you sign — and your signature certifies, under penalty of perjury, that your answers are true. If something in your history worries you, say it before filing, not after.

Source: 8 CFR §292.1 (who may represent applicants) — see Trust & Compliance · General information, not legal advice.

7 · After you file, up front

  • Receipt number: USCIS mails receipt notices (Form I-797C) with a receipt number for each form — that number is your key to every tracker. Keep it.
  • Track in one place: the Case Tracker translates USCIS statuses into plain English; the NVC / CEAC Tracker follows consular cases; DOL and EOIR statuses are explained alongside — USCIS, NVC, DOL, and EOIR, one hub.
  • What statuses mean: "Case Was Received" (in line) → "Biometrics appointment scheduled" → "Case Is Being Actively Reviewed" → "Interview Was Scheduled" → "Case Approved" / "Card Was Mailed" — or an RFE or a denial. Each one is translated on the tracker page, with what to do next.
  • Notices to expect: receipts, biometrics, possibly an RFE, the interview notice, and the decision. Every notice with a date on it is a deadline.
  • If USCIS denies the case: read the denial notice first — it says whether you may appeal or file a motion (Form I-290B, on a short deadline printed in the notice), whether refiling is possible, and what changed facts would matter. Denial strategy is legal work: see If Denied? and get an attorney before the deadline runs.

Example: A denial notice gives 30 days to file Form I-290B. The family spends three of those weeks asking friends what to do — and reaches an attorney with days left. The notice told them the deadline on day one: read every USCIS letter the day it arrives, and act on the date printed on it.

Source: USCIS form and notice instructions, including Form I-290B — uscis.gov/i-290b ↗ · General information, not legal advice.

What Immigration Says About Money, Debts, and Filing for Someone

When you file for a family member, you are not only sending forms — you are making money promises to the U.S. government, and the government writes down exactly what those promises mean. This page explains, in plain English, what USCIS and the law actually say about the money side of filing: the sponsor's contract, debts, taxes, child support, public benefits, and filing fees. Every claim below names its official source so you can check it yourself, and every section has a real example.

General information, not legal advice. This page explains published government rules in plain English. It is not legal advice for your case, and NIPTEI is a document preparation service, not a law firm. If your situation involves a debt, a benefit, a denial, or any red-flag history, talk to a licensed immigration attorney or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit before you file. No one can guarantee that a petition or visa will be approved.

1 · The Affidavit of Support (Form I-864) is a legally enforceable contract

When a sponsor signs Form I-864, Affidavit of Support, they are not filling in a formality — they are signing a contract under section 213A of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA). In that contract, the sponsor promises to provide the immigrant they sponsor with enough support to keep them at 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for the household size. For 2026, that is $41,250 for a household of 4 and $27,050 for a household of 2 (check your own household size on the Sponsor Qualifier).

How long the promise lasts. The sponsor's duty normally ends only when the sponsored immigrant: becomes a U.S. citizen; is credited with 40 qualifying quarters of work (about 10 years); dies; permanently leaves the United States; or loses lawful permanent resident status. Getting divorced does not end the duty — a sponsor who divorces the immigrant they sponsored still owes the obligation.

Who can enforce it. Two parties can sue the sponsor in court to enforce the contract: the sponsored immigrant, and any federal, state, or local government agency — or private entity — that gave the immigrant a means-tested public benefit.

Example: Marie sponsors her husband; their household of 4 must be maintained at the $41,250 line. Three years later they separate, and her husband receives means-tested benefits. The agency that paid can demand repayment from Marie — and if she refuses, the agency (and her husband) can sue her on the I-864 contract, even though they are no longer together.

Source: USCIS Form I-864 and its instructions, INA §213A — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗

2 · If the sponsor does not pay, and the immigrant needs help

The I-864 does not block the immigrant from asking for help. A sponsored immigrant may apply for means-tested public benefits (cash assistance, food assistance, medical coverage, and similar programs). Whether they receive them is the benefit agency's decision — but two money rules follow them:

  • Deeming: when the agency decides if the immigrant qualifies, the sponsor's income and resources are counted ("deemed") as the immigrant's in most cases — so the sponsor's money can make the immigrant ineligible, even if the sponsor is not actually giving it.
  • Repayment: if the immigrant does receive means-tested benefits, the agency can ask the sponsor to repay the cost. If the sponsor does not repay after being asked, the agency can sue the sponsor to collect.

Example: A sponsor stops helping the immigrant he sponsored. She applies for food assistance. The agency counts his income as if it were hers (deeming). If she still receives benefits, the agency bills him for the value of those benefits — and can take him to court if he does not pay.

Source: USCIS Form I-864 instructions (sponsor's obligations, deeming, and agency reimbursement) — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗

3 · Public charge — what USCIS actually looks at now

"Public charge" is the ground in INA §212(a)(4) under which USCIS can deny a green card to someone it finds likely at any time to become a public charge. DHS published a final rule in the Federal Register on July 20, 2026 that rescinded the 2022 public charge regulations, effective September 18, 2026, and USCIS issued updated Policy Manual guidance to match. Here is what USCIS says it looks at now:

  • The five factors Congress wrote into the law: the applicant's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills. The officer may also consider the Form I-864 Affidavit of Support when one is required.
  • Benefits received before September 18, 2026: USCIS considers only public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense.
  • Benefits received on or after September 18, 2026: USCIS says it will consider any and all means-tested public benefits — its guidance names examples such as cash assistance for income maintenance, housing assistance, food stamps, and financial aid for college.
  • It is a totality-of-the-circumstances decision: the officer weighs everything together, case by case. No single factor decides it — other than a missing required I-864, which can cause a denial on its own.

Example: Two applicants have the same income. One is young, healthy, skilled, and has a sponsor whose I-864 comfortably meets 125%. The other has no sponsor support and a long history of cash assistance. USCIS does not compare one number — it weighs the whole picture for each person, and the outcomes can differ.

Good Moral Character connection: USCIS's November 4, 2026 Good Moral Character guidance — covering tax compliance, child support, I-864 compliance, and public benefits — is explained in our News & Deadlines coverage. Read it there; we do not repeat it here as a separate claim.

Source: USCIS, "USCIS Issues Guidance on Making Public Charge Inadmissibility Determination" — uscis.gov ↗ · The final rule was published in the Federal Register — federalregister.gov ↗

4 · Debts and money the immigrant or the sponsor owes

People ask us one question in many forms: "I owe money — can I still file?" Here is what USCIS actually says, debt by debt — including where USCIS does not say a debt blocks anything.

Taxes owed. USCIS asks about tax filing and tax debts on its forms, and for naturalization (Form N-400), failure to file required tax returns — or an unpaid tax debt with no payment arrangement — can be treated as a lack of Good Moral Character. Under the November 4, 2026 guidance (see News & Deadlines), tax compliance is one of the things USCIS weighs. Example: a green-card holder who has not filed taxes for three years applies for citizenship. USCIS can deny on Good Moral Character grounds until the returns are filed and the debt is on a payment plan.

Child support owed. For N-400, willfully failing to support your dependents can be a Good Moral Character problem — and per the November 4, 2026 guidance, that includes unpaid child support even when there is no court order. Example: a father who informally agreed to support his children and stopped paying can face a citizenship denial even though no judge ever ordered the payments.

Unpaid USCIS fees. This one is mechanical and immediate: if the correct USCIS fee does not arrive with the filing, USCIS rejects the filing — it is not accepted, no receipt number is issued, and no case exists (see section 5 below).

A sponsor who owes money. Owing debts does not by itself disqualify a sponsor. For the I-864, what USCIS measures is the sponsor's current income against the 125% line — and, if income is short, their assets, counted at 3× the shortfall for a spouse or minor child of a U.S. citizen and 5× for most other cases. USCIS does not say that a debt alone blocks a filing or a sponsorship. Example: a sponsor with $8,000 of credit-card debt and a steady $45,000 salary for a household of 4 still qualifies on income — the debt is not the test; the income is.

Bankruptcy and court judgments. USCIS does not state this — do not assume it: USCIS does not publish a rule that a bankruptcy, or a civil money judgment by itself, makes an applicant inadmissible or disqualifies a sponsor. What is always dangerous is not the debt — it is lying about anything on a signed form (see section 6). If a debt involves fraud, taxes, or a court case, ask an attorney before filing; that is a legal question, not a clerical one.

Sources: USCIS Form I-864 and Sponsor Qualifier rules — uscis.gov/i-864 ↗ · Good Moral Character coverage with the November 4, 2026 guidance — News & Deadlines

5 · Filing fees — and what happens if you do not pay them

  • How USCIS fees are paid in our packets: electronically, with Form G-1450 (credit/debit card) or Form G-1650 (ACH bank transfer) — no paper checks. The card or account must actually have the money or credit available; a declined card is the same as no payment.
  • If the fee is wrong, missing, or declined: USCIS rejects the filing. You receive a rejection notice, the packet is returned, no receipt number is issued, and legally it is as if you never filed — filing dates, deadlines, and status tied to that filing are not protected. You must correct the payment (and the form edition, if that was also wrong) and file again.
  • Fees are not refunded because a case is denied. USCIS states that its filing fees are non-refundable regardless of the decision — the fee pays for USCIS to process the case, not for an approval. A denial does not come with your money back.
  • USCIS fees are never our fee. Government fees are paid to USCIS; our service fee is paid to your preparer. They are always shown in two separate columns on this site and are never combined into one number.

Example: A family mails an I-485 with a G-1450 for the old fee amount. USCIS rejects the whole packet — no receipt, no case, no place in line. The family refiles with the correct $1,440 paper-filing fee and the mandatory 09/18/26 edition. If USCIS later denies that application on its merits, the $1,440 is not refunded.

Sources: USCIS filing-fee schedule, Form G-1055 — uscis.gov/g-1055 ↗ · Form G-1450 — uscis.gov/g-1450 ↗

6 · What filing for someone means for the person who files

  • You sign under penalty of perjury. Every USCIS form's certification says, in substance, that the information is complete, true, and correct, and that you authorize USCIS to verify it. Signing a form you know contains false information can lead to denial, revocation of an approval already granted, and criminal penalties for fraud or false statements.
  • The petitioner answers for the petition. The person who files for a relative is responsible for the truth of what they sign — including the I-864 contract in section 1, which can be enforced in court.
  • Address changes are legal duties, not courtesies. The immigrant must report a new address to USCIS on Form AR-11 within 10 days of moving. A sponsor must report their own new address on Form I-865 within 30 days of moving — for as long as the I-864 duty lasts. Missed mail has ended cases: a biometrics or interview notice sent to an old address does not stop the clock.

Example: A petitioner guesses at his brother's prior addresses "to make the form look complete." The guesses contradict the brother's own filings. That is not a clerical error — it is a false statement on a signed certification, and it can take down both cases. Never guess: write what is true, and say "unknown" where the form allows it.

Sources: the certification printed on every USCIS form — uscis.gov ↗ · Form I-865, Sponsor's Notice of Change of Address — uscis.gov/i-865 ↗ · AR-11 — see the AR-11 Helper

7 · "What could happen" — the plain-English summary

If this happens…What USCIS / the government can doWhat to do next
You sign the I-864 and the immigrant receives means-tested benefitsThe benefit agency can demand repayment from you, and the immigrant or the agency can sue you on the contractRead section 1 before you sign. If you cannot carry the duty, talk to an attorney first — do not sign and hope

Something on a signed form is not trueDenial, revocation of an approval, and possible criminal penaltiesNever sign what you have not read. Correct the record with an attorney's help
Red-flag history: entered without inspection, overstay, prior removal, arrest, prior denialFiling can expose the person to enforcement or a denial instead of a benefitPause — legal help is strongly recommended first. Run the Danger Shield, then choose your help: DIY ($25 per form), a document preparer (clerical only), a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit — the choice is yours, and an attorney's review protects you and the case

The same rules, answered question by question — including the widow(er) route when a citizen sponsor has died — are in Ask NIPTEI — Financial Obligation and Ask NIPTEI — Widow / Widower Green Card.

Check the Sponsor Qualifier Read the Family Filing Guides Before You File — Know Everything In Advance

If the person you would file with — or file for — is abusing you, money is not your only problem, and you are not trapped. An abused spouse, child, or parent of a U.S. citizen or green card holder can self-petition under VAWA (Form I-360, USCIS fee $0) without the abuser's help or knowledge — and a VAWA self-petitioner does not need the abuser to sign an I-864 for them. Victims of crimes and trafficking have their own doors. Read: Domestic Violence — How to Get a Green Card on Your Own (VAWA) · U Visa & T Visa — Victims of Crime & Trafficking. In danger now? Call 911 · National Domestic Violence Hotline 1-800-799-7233.

People also ask — money, debts, and filing for someone

What is the affidavit of support income for 2026? 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (Form I-864P, 2026): household of 2 — $27,050; household of 4 — $41,250; each extra person +$7,100. Check yours in the Sponsor Qualifier.

Is the I-864 really a contract? Yes — the sponsor promises support at 125% of the guidelines and can be sued by the immigrant or by an agency that paid means-tested benefits. See section 1 of this page and Ask NIPTEI — Financial Obligation.

Does owing money stop me from filing or sponsoring? USCIS does not state that a debt alone disqualifies a sponsor — income and assets against the 125% line are the test. Unpaid taxes or child support can hurt a later N-400 citizenship case. See section 4 of this page.

What happens if I miss a payment on my plan? On this platform, our published rule is: “If you miss a payment, 50% is added to the total amount.” (example: $999 → +$499.50 → $1,498.50). USCIS fees are separate and are never part of the installment plan.

This page is general information about published government rules, with the official source named for each claim. It is not legal advice, and it does not promise any outcome. Where USCIS does not state a rule, this page says so — please do the same when you explain these topics to family and friends.

Domestic Violence — How to Get a Green Card on Your Own (VAWA)

🛡 Safe place — use this page safely. If someone is watching your phone, or may check it later, tap Quick Exit: this page disappears and Google opens instead. NIPTEI keeps no case details on the home screen for VAWA, U, T, and asylum clients, and USCIS keeps these cases confidential by law (8 U.S.C. §1367).

✕ Quick Exit — leave this page now

How to get a green card if your husband, wife, parent, or adult child abuses you: if the person hurting you is a U.S. citizen or green card holder who is your spouse, parent, or child, you may not need them at all. The VAWA green card — a self-petition on Form I-360 — lets you file for yourself, in secret, and work toward your own green card. This page explains the domestic violence green card in plain English: who qualifies, how to file I-360, what documents are needed, three home examples step by step, what happens after you file, and how to file safely. General information, not legal advice.

SAFETY FIRST — read this before anything else.
If you are in danger now, call 911.
National Domestic Violence Hotline: call 1-800-799-7233 (TTY 1-800-787-3224) · text “START” to 88788 · thehotline.org ↗ — free, confidential, 24/7, in many languages. The Hotline can help you make a safety plan and find shelter and local help.
Do NOT contact the abuser for documents. You do not need the abuser's permission, signature, or papers to file VAWA. USCIS keeps a VAWA case confidential and does NOT tell the abuser you filed — federal law (8 U.S.C. §1367) protects VAWA, T, and U case information, and USCIS mails everything to the safe address you choose. NIPTEI will never contact the abuser.

1 · What VAWA is

The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) is a federal law that protects immigrants who are being abused by a close family member who is a U.S. citizen or green card holder. Normally, that family member controls the immigration process — they file the petition, and they can threaten to withdraw it. VAWA breaks that control: certain abused spouses, children, and parents may self-petition — file Form I-360 for themselves — without the abuser knowing, without the abuser's help, and without the abuser filing for them. Despite the law's name, VAWA is not only for women: an abused husband, son, or father with the qualifying relationship can self-petition too. If USCIS approves the I-360, the self-petitioner can then apply for a green card (Form I-485 inside the U.S., or consular processing abroad). The USCIS fee for a VAWA Form I-360 is $0 — there is no filing fee for VAWA self-petitioners. (Other I-360 categories are different: USCIS lists $515 for most other I-360 categories, and $0 for VAWA and SIJS — always confirm on Form G-1055 at uscis.gov/fees before filing.)

Example: a husband files an I-130 for his wife, then threatens to withdraw it every time she disagrees with him. She does not have to wait for him or beg him. She can file her own I-360 under VAWA, and his I-130 no longer controls her future.

Sources: USCIS, Abused Spouses, Children and Parents (VAWA) — uscis.gov ↗ · Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

2 · Who qualifies — and a home example for each

VAWA has a short list of relationships. You must show: the qualifying relationship, that the abuser is (or was) a U.S. citizen or green card holder, that you were subjected to battery or extreme cruelty, that you lived with the abuser, and that you are a person of good moral character. A spouse must also show the marriage was entered in good faith — a real marriage, not a marriage only for papers.

Abused spouse of a U.S. citizen

You may self-petition if you are, or were, married to a U.S. citizen who abused you — or who abused your child. You may include your unmarried children under 21 on your petition. You can also still qualify in some situations after the marriage ended: for example, if the marriage ended in a divorce connected to the abuse within the 2 years before filing, or the citizen spouse died within the 2 years before filing — an attorney should check the dates, because they are strict. Because a U.S. citizen's spouse is an immediate relative, a visa is immediately available — the I-485 can often be filed with the I-360 or while it is pending.

Home example: Denise's husband is a U.S. citizen. He keeps her passport, forbids her to work, and hits her when she talks about leaving. Denise files Form I-360 herself, with her own statement, photos, and a letter from her sister. He is never told.

Abused spouse of a green card holder

The same door exists if your abusive spouse is a lawful permanent resident (green card holder) instead of a citizen. You file the same Form I-360 at $0, and you may include your unmarried children under 21. The difference is timing: spouses of green card holders are in a family preference category, so the green card step (I-485) waits until a visa number is available — but after the I-360 is approved, USCIS may grant deferred action, and with deferred action you can apply for a work permit (Form I-765) while you wait.

Home example: a wife whose husband holds a green card files her I-360 with her young daughter included. Her I-360 is approved, she receives deferred action, applies for a work permit, and works legally while her visa number comes up — then she files the I-485. (This is Jean's full story in section 3 below.)

Abused child — and abused stepchild — of a U.S. citizen or green card holder

An abused child may self-petition if they are under 21 and unmarried and were abused by their U.S. citizen or green card holder parent. An abused stepchild can also qualify as a “child” when the step-relationship exists — the details of when the marriage that created the step-relationship happened matter, so an attorney should confirm them for your family. A child may even file after turning 21 but before turning 25 if they can show the abuse was the main reason for the delay in filing. A child self-petitioner may include their own unmarried children under 21.

Home example: a 17-year-old whose green-card-holder stepfather beats him files his own I-360 with the help of his school counselor and an attorney. He does not need his stepfather's signature on anything.

Abused parent of a U.S. citizen

A parent may self-petition if they were abused by their U.S. citizen son or daughter who is 21 or older. (There is no VAWA parent category for the parent of a green card holder — the adult child must be a U.S. citizen.) One difference to know: a parent self-petitioner cannot include derivative children on the petition — each person files their own case.

Home example: a mother lives with her 30-year-old U.S. citizen son, who screams at her, takes her money, and has pushed her against a wall. She files Form I-360 herself. Her son is never told.

Abused fiancé(e) — the K-1 door, and its limit

If you entered the U.S. on a K-1 fiancé(e) visa and married the U.S. citizen who filed for you within 90 days, and that spouse then abused you, you are an abused spouse of a U.S. citizen — the VAWA door above can fit you, even though a K-1 spouse normally must adjust status through that same petitioner. If you did NOT marry the petitioner within 90 days — or never married them at all — VAWA does not fit that relationship, because there is no qualifying marriage. Do not guess and do not wait: get a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit immediately — a U visa or another form of relief may fit instead, and deadlines may be running.

Home example: a woman enters on a K-1, marries her citizen fiancé on day 40, and he becomes violent. She can self-petition under VAWA as his abused spouse. Her friend, whose fiancé refused to marry her and sent her away on day 95, cannot use VAWA for that relationship — she needs an attorney to check the U visa and other options right away.

What if the abuser is NOT a spouse, parent, or child?

Say it plainly: VAWA does NOT cover every abuser. VAWA covers only a U.S. citizen or green card holder who is your spouse, parent, or child (and a K-1 spouse you actually married). VAWA does not cover a brother or sister, a boyfriend or girlfriend you never married, an employer, or another relative — no matter how serious the abuse is. That does not mean nothing can help. Depending on the facts, other doors may fit: a U visa (Form I-918) if you were the victim of a qualifying crime and help law enforcement; a T visa (Form I-914) if you were a victim of human trafficking; asylum if you fear persecution in your home country; or other relief an attorney identifies. Which one fits is a legal decision — an attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit must check your facts. Do not guess, and do not pay anyone who guesses. The U and T visas are explained on our U Visa & T Visa page.

Home example: a man is beaten and robbed by his brother, a green card holder. VAWA cannot help him — a brother is not a VAWA relationship. But the beating and robbery are crimes: a U visa may fit, because he reported them and cooperated with the police.

Source: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Immigration Options for Victims of Crime — dhs.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

3 · Three home examples — step by step

Example 1 · Maria — married to a U.S. citizen husband who hits her

What happened: Maria married a U.S. citizen. He never filed any papers for her. He hits her, takes her phone, and threatens: “I will call immigration if you leave.”

What she did, step by step:

  1. Safety first. From a friend's phone, Maria called the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) and made a safety plan. She did not tell her husband anything about immigration.
  2. Legal help. A DOJ-accredited nonprofit reviewed her case free and confirmed VAWA fit. NIPTEI's preparers later supported the clerical packet alongside the nonprofit — nobody from NIPTEI ever contacted her husband.
  3. Documents — gathered without him. Her marriage certificate (a certified copy ordered from the county — she did not ask him), photos of the certificate she already had on her phone, her own detailed written statement of the abuse, photos of bruises, threatening text messages, a letter from her cousin who had seen the abuse, and a police report from the one night a neighbor called 911. For proof of his citizenship, she had a photo of his U.S. passport from a family trip; the nonprofit told her that even without it, USCIS can check its own records — she should never go back to the house to hunt for papers.
  4. She filed Form I-360 herself — USCIS fee $0 — using her friend's address as her safe mailing address, and she checked the box on the I-360 asking USCIS to consider her for a work permit if approved. Because her husband is a U.S. citizen, she is an immediate relative, so she also filed Form I-485 (paper filing, USCIS fee $1,440) with a Form I-765 work permit request while the I-360 was pending.
  5. What happened next: USCIS mailed a Notice of Prima Facie Case to her safe address — her husband received nothing and was never told. Her I-360 was approved; her work permit arrived; her I-485 was approved and she received her own green card — without his help, his signature, or his knowledge.

Maria is an example, not a promise — every case is decided on its own facts. Source: USCIS, VAWA — uscis.gov ↗.

Example 2 · Jean — abused wife of a green card holder, with a child

What happened: Jean's husband has a green card. He controls all the money, screams at her daily, has shoved her, and threatens to “send her back” and keep their 6-year-old daughter.

What she did, step by step:

  1. Safety first. Jean texted “START” to 88788 from a coworker's phone and connected with a local shelter advocate, who helped her plan and keep copies of documents outside the home.
  2. She filed Form I-360 herself — USCIS fee $0 — and included her daughter (under 21, unmarried) as a derivative on the petition. Her documents: marriage certificate, her daughter's birth certificate, a photo of her husband's green card she already had, her written statement, medical records from an emergency-room visit, and a letter from her pastor.
  3. Prima facie notice. USCIS sent a Notice of Prima Facie Case to her safe address. As a spouse self-petitioner with prima facie eligibility, she could show that notice when applying for certain public benefits she qualified for.
  4. Approval, deferred action, work permit. Her I-360 was approved. Because spouses of green card holders wait for a visa number, USCIS granted her deferred action, and with it she filed Form I-765 and received a work permit — so she could work legally and support herself and her daughter while waiting.
  5. Green card. When her visa number became available, she filed Form I-485 (paper filing, USCIS fee $1,440) for herself and her daughter, and both received green cards. Her husband was never told about any of it.

Jean is an example, not a promise. Source: USCIS, VAWA — uscis.gov ↗.

Example 3 · A child abused by a U.S. citizen parent — and a parent abused by a U.S. citizen adult child

Part A — the child. Daniel, 16, lives with his U.S. citizen father, who beats him and locks him out of the house. Daniel's aunt and a school social worker helped him reach an attorney. Daniel filed Form I-360 for himself as an abused child (under 21, unmarried) — with his birth certificate showing the relationship, school and medical records, and statements from his aunt and counselor. A child or the child's trusted adult helper does not need the abusive parent's permission to file. His I-360 was approved, and as the child of a U.S. citizen he could move to the green card step (Form I-485) without a quota wait.

Part B — the parent. Mrs. Pierre, 62, lives with her U.S. citizen daughter, age 34, who takes her pension money, forbids her visitors, and has slapped her. Mrs. Pierre filed Form I-360 for herself as an abused parent of a U.S. citizen — with her daughter's birth certificate (showing Mrs. Pierre as the mother) and proof of her daughter's citizenship, her own statement, and a letter from her church. Parents cannot add derivative children to a VAWA petition, so her case was hers alone. It was approved, and she filed Form I-485 for her green card. Her daughter was never told.

Daniel and Mrs. Pierre are examples, not promises. Source: USCIS, VAWA — uscis.gov ↗.

4 · What is needed — the document checklist

USCIS must consider any credible evidence you submit for a VAWA case — there is no single required document that can sink you if it does not exist. Build the strongest packet you honestly can:

  • Proof of the relationship: marriage certificate (spouse), birth certificate naming the parent (child or parent cases), plus proof any prior marriages ended (divorce decree or death certificate).
  • Proof the abuser is a U.S. citizen or green card holder: a copy of their U.S. passport, birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or green card — if you have it. If you do not have it: do not contact the abuser and do not go back for it. Give USCIS what you know (full name, date of birth, and an A-number if you know it) — USCIS can check its own records, and your attorney can help with this piece.
  • Proof you lived together: a lease with both names, utility bills, mail to the same address, tax returns, insurance, or letters from people who know you lived together.
  • Proof of the abuse (battery or extreme cruelty): police reports if any exist, medical or hospital records, photos of injuries or damage, threatening texts, emails, or voicemails, court or protective-order records, shelter or counselor records, and letters (declarations) from people who saw the abuse or its effects. You do NOT need a police report to file. Abuse is also more than hitting: threats about immigration status, isolation, taking money or documents, and controlling behavior can be part of extreme cruelty.
  • Your own detailed statement: your written declaration — who, what, when, where, how often, and how it affected you — counts as evidence. For many people it is the center of the case. Write what is true, in your own words; your attorney or preparer can help you organize it, never invent it.
  • Proof of good moral character: commonly a local police clearance or statement from where you have lived, plus your own declaration — an attorney will tell you what fits your history.
  • For a spouse: proof the marriage was real (good faith): joint accounts, lease, tax returns, insurance, photos over time, children's birth certificates, statements from people who knew you as a couple.
  • Certified English translations of any document not in English, with the translator's signed certificate.

If a document is missing: explain in writing what is missing and what honest steps you took to get it, and use other credible evidence in its place. Never invent a document, never buy one, and never use a false document — a false document can destroy the case and create far worse problems. A missing document is a problem to explain; a fake document is a disaster.

Source: USCIS, Form I-360 — uscis.gov/i-360 ↗. General information, not legal advice.

5 · What happens after you file

  • Receipt and safe mail. USCIS sends your receipt to the safe address on your petition — never to the abuser. VAWA cases are handled by a specialized USCIS unit, and your information is protected by law (8 U.S.C. §1367).
  • Prima facie determination. If your filing shows basic (prima facie) eligibility, USCIS issues a Notice of Prima Facie Case. Spouses and children who self-petition are treated as “qualified aliens” who may use that notice to apply for certain public benefits; parent self-petitioners are not eligible for benefits on that basis.
  • Approval. An approved I-360 gives you immigrant classification — it is the key, and the green card application is the next step. It does not by itself give you status or a work permit.
  • Deferred action. If you are in the U.S. and your I-360 is approved, USCIS may grant deferred action (case by case) — protection from removal for a period — especially important while a preference-category visa number is not yet available.
  • Work permit (Form I-765). If you checked the box on the I-360 asking for employment authorization, USCIS automatically considers you for a work permit when the I-360 is approved — no separate I-765 is needed for that first permit. If you did not check the box, or you have deferred action, you file Form I-765 to ask for the permit. Your included children can also apply for work permits with Form I-765 after approval.
  • The green card. If a visa is immediately available (always true for immediate relatives of U.S. citizens), you may file Form I-485 (paper filing, USCIS fee $1,440) together with the I-360, while it is pending, or after approval. If you must wait for a visa number (most green-card-holder spouse/child cases), you file the I-485 when your number is current. If you are outside the U.S., the approved petition goes to the National Visa Center for consular processing.
  • Interview. USCIS may call some self-petitioners for an interview. The notice comes to your safe address, and officers who conduct these interviews have specialized training and follow VAWA confidentiality protections. Show up — missing an interview you were told about can cause a denial.
  • If the abuser tries to withdraw “their” petition: it does not control you. Your I-360 is your own case, not theirs. An abuser withdrawing an I-130, refusing to attend an interview, or calling USCIS cannot withdraw, cancel, or veto your VAWA self-petition — and USCIS may not decide your case based only on information the abuser provides. Filing VAWA gives the abuser no way to stop you.

Source: USCIS, VAWA — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

6 · What can happen to the abuser?

Read this carefully, because many people stay silent out of fear of this answer: filing VAWA does not automatically arrest the abuser, deport the abuser, or take the abuser's green card or citizenship. USCIS does not notify the abuser that you filed, and your I-360 is about your immigration status — it is not a criminal case against them. Anything criminal is separate: if the abuser is arrested, charged, or ordered by a court to stay away from you (a protective order), that happens through the police and the courts, because of what they did — not because you filed a VAWA petition. Any immigration effect on the abuser would come from that separate criminal case, not from your I-360. The National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) can explain protective orders and local legal help, confidentially and free.

Example: a woman files VAWA and worries her husband will be deported and her children will blame her. Her attorney explains: her I-360 asks USCIS for her own green card. It sends no one to his door. If police ever act, it will be because of his own conduct and a separate case.

7 · How to file safely

  • Use a safe mailing address — a trusted friend, relative, shelter, or your attorney's office. You do not have to live at the safe address for USCIS to mail your case there. Keep it current with USCIS using the special address-change procedures for VAWA/T/U cases.
  • Use a safe email and phone the abuser cannot see. Do not read case messages on a shared phone or computer the abuser checks.
  • On a shared device, use a private browser window and clear your history afterward if it is safe to do so — or use a library, shelter, or advocate's computer instead.
  • Keep copies of your documents outside the home — photos on a safe account, or paper copies with a trusted person.
  • Do not tell the abuser you filed, and do not ask the abuser for any document, signature, or money for the case.
  • NIPTEI will never contact the abuser — not for documents, not for money, not for any reason. Tell us your safe contact method and we will use only that.

These cases involve legal analysis and legal help is strongly recommended — especially VAWA, U visa, T visa, and widow(er) cases — and an attorney's legal review protects you, the preparer, and the case. But the choice is yours: you may file alone, or use a document preparer, or get an attorney or DOJ representative. If you choose DIY or a preparer, we strongly recommend you also get an attorney to review it — Review $99 per form, Human Review $199.

People also ask — VAWA green card

How to get a green card if your husband abuses you? If he is a U.S. citizen or green card holder, you can self-petition under VAWA on Form I-360 — without his knowledge or help — then apply for the green card on Form I-485. Full steps are on this page.

How to file I-360 for VAWA? File Form I-360 with evidence of the relationship, the abuser's status, living together, the abuse, and good moral character. USCIS fee for VAWA: $0. Your own written statement counts as evidence, and you do not need a police report.

Will USCIS tell my spouse I filed VAWA? No. VAWA cases are confidential by law (8 U.S.C. §1367). USCIS mails everything to your safe address and does not notify the abuser.

Can a husband file VAWA too? Yes. VAWA self-petitions are open to abused spouses, children, and parents of any gender with the qualifying relationship.

What if my abuser is my boyfriend, brother, or boss? VAWA does not cover that relationship. A U visa (crime victims), a T visa (trafficking), or asylum may fit instead — an attorney or DOJ nonprofit must check which one.

Does VAWA have a deadline like the widow(er) I-360? They are different cases that share Form I-360. The 2-year deadline belongs to the widow(er) route (2 years from the citizen spouse's death) — do not confuse them. VAWA has its own timing traps (for example, a divorce connected to the abuse, or filing at ages 21–25 as a child), which is one more reason to get legal help early.

Rules can change. USCIS revised its VAWA Policy Manual guidance on December 22, 2025, and that revision applies to pending and new petitions. This page explains the rules in plain English as published — confirm the current guidance at uscis.gov ↗ and with your attorney before you file. General information, not legal advice.

U Visa — If You Were a Victim of a Crime, You May Qualify for a Green Card

🛡 Safe place — use this page safely. If someone is watching your phone, or may check it later, tap Quick Exit: this page disappears and Google opens instead. This page covers the U visa and the T visa, and the same safe way of reading applies to asylum clients: NIPTEI keeps no case details on the home screen for VAWA, U, T, and asylum clients, and these cases are confidential by law (8 U.S.C. §1367).

✕ Quick Exit — leave this page now

The U visa green card path, in plain English: if you were the victim of a crime in the United States — domestic violence, sexual assault, a violent attack, robbery, extortion, trafficking, or another qualifying crime — and you helped the police or prosecutors, the U visa (Form I-918) may protect you, give you a work permit, and after 3 years let you apply for a green card. This page explains U visa requirements, what is needed, the honest wait (the 10,000-per-year cap), a step-by-step home example, family members, and — in the last section — the T visa for victims of human trafficking. General information, not legal advice.

Confidential, by law. Information in a U visa (and T visa or VAWA) case is strictly confidential and protected by law (8 U.S.C. §1367). You may use a safe mailing address on your petition — you do not have to live there. In danger now? Call 911. National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233 (TTY 1-800-787-3224), text “START” to 88788. National Human Trafficking Hotline: 1-888-373-7888.

1 · What a U visa is — and the 4 things you must show

The U visa (U nonimmigrant status) was created by Congress in 2000 to protect crime victims and to help law enforcement investigate and prosecute crimes. You may qualify if all four are true:

  1. You are the victim of a qualifying criminal activity (see the list below).
  2. You suffered substantial physical or mental abuse because of the crime.
  3. You have information about the crime — and you were helpful, are helpful, or are likely to be helpful to law enforcement in investigating or prosecuting it. (If you are under 16 or cannot provide information because of a disability, a parent, guardian, or “next friend” can hold the information and help on your behalf.)
  4. The crime happened in the United States or violated U.S. laws.

You must also be admissible to the U.S. — if you are not, many problems can be waived on Form I-192, which is one reason these cases need an attorney. Qualifying crimes include: domestic violence, sexual assault, rape, abusive sexual contact, felonious assault, kidnapping, false imprisonment, hostage-taking, blackmail, extortion, robbery-type crimes, stalking, torture, manslaughter, murder, trafficking, involuntary servitude, slave trade, peonage, fraud in foreign labor contracting, prostitution, sexual exploitation, female genital mutilation, incest, obstruction of justice, perjury, witness tampering, unlawful criminal restraint, and abduction — and attempts, conspiracies, and similar crimes can count too. If your crime is not named word-for-word, do not give up: an attorney checks whether it is “substantially similar” to a listed crime.

Example: a store clerk is shot during a robbery, survives, identifies the robber for the police, and testifies. He has nightmares and cannot work for months. Crime + substantial harm + cooperation: this is the shape of a U visa case.

Source: USCIS, Victims of Criminal Activity: U Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

2 · Home example — Ana, step by step

Ana's story: from victim to green card

What happened: Ana lived with her boyfriend, who beat her repeatedly and threatened her children. They never married — so VAWA could not help her (a boyfriend is not a VAWA relationship). One night, a neighbor called 911.

What she did, step by step:

  1. She cooperated. Ana gave the police a statement, let them photograph her injuries, and answered the prosecutor's questions. She kept copies of the police report and her hospital record.
  2. Legal help. A DOJ-accredited nonprofit attorney reviewed her case and confirmed the U visa fit: domestic violence is a qualifying crime, she had suffered substantial abuse, and she had been helpful.
  3. The certification. Her attorney asked the police agency to complete Form I-918, Supplement B — the Law Enforcement Certification confirming she was a victim and was helpful. An authorized official signed it. (The certification is time-sensitive — it must be signed within the 6 months before the I-918 is filed — so her attorney filed promptly.)
  4. She filed Form I-918 with the Supplement B, her own detailed statement, the police and medical records, and Supplement A petitions for her spouse and her unmarried children under 21. USCIS fee: $0 — U visa petitions and related forms are fee-exempt, all the way through the green card.
  5. The wait — with protection. Because of the yearly cap (section 4 below), Ana waited. USCIS reviewed her petition, found it bona fide (genuine and complete on its face), and granted her deferred action and a work permit while she waited for a U visa number.
  6. U status. When her turn came, Ana received U nonimmigrant status for 4 years. As the main (principal) applicant, her work permit was issued with the approval.
  7. The green card. After 3 years of continuous presence in the U.S. in U status — and having not refused reasonable requests for help from law enforcement — Ana filed Form I-485 and received her green card. Her family members filed their own I-485s as they qualified.

Ana is an example, not a promise — timelines and outcomes depend on the facts and on the yearly cap. Source: USCIS, U Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗.

3 · What is needed — the U visa checklist

  • Form I-918, Petition for U Nonimmigrant Status — USCIS fee $0 (U petitions and related forms are fee-exempt through adjustment of status; confirm on Form G-1055).
  • Form I-918, Supplement B — the Law Enforcement Certification, signed by an authorized official of a certifying agency (for example, a police department, prosecutor's office, or judge). This certification is required — without it, there is no U visa — and it must be signed within the 6 months before you file.
  • Your own statement describing the crime and the harm it caused you, in your own words.
  • Proof of the crime and the abuse: police reports, charging documents or court records, medical or mental-health records, photos, and letters from advocates, counselors, or witnesses.
  • Form I-192 waiver, if you have inadmissibility problems (for example, entry without inspection or prior immigration violations) — an attorney must review this with you.
  • Form I-918, Supplement A for each qualifying family member (section 5).
  • Certified English translations of anything not in English.

What if the police will not sign the certification? Be honest with yourself about this: no signed Supplement B means no U visa — USCIS cannot grant one without it. But one “no” is not always the end. A different official or agency may be able to certify (police, prosecutors, judges, and certain other authorities can be certifying agencies), and an attorney or DOJ nonprofit can make a proper, documented request — sometimes to a supervisor or a designated certifying official — and can also check whether VAWA, a T visa, or asylum fits you better. Do not pay anyone who promises they can “make” an agency sign.

Source: USCIS, U Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

4 · The wait — the 10,000 cap, the waiting list, and the bona fide determination

How long does a U visa take? Honestly: it can take years, and anyone who promises you a fast green card this way is not telling you the truth. By law, only 10,000 U visas may be granted to main (principal) applicants each year — family members do not count against the cap. Far more people apply than 10,000, so a line forms. Here is how the wait works:

  • Bona fide determination: while your I-918 is pending, USCIS reviews whether it is bona fide — complete and genuine on its face. If so, USCIS can grant you (and your included family members in the U.S.) deferred action and you can receive a work permit while you wait for a visa number.
  • Waiting list: if the cap is reached, approvable petitions go on a waiting list. People on the waiting list receive deferred action or parole and may apply for work authorization. When visas free up, they are given out in the order petitions were received — you do not have to ask again; USCIS notifies you.
  • U status itself lasts 4 years once granted (extensions exist in limited situations, including while a green card application is pending).

Example: a father files a complete I-918 in a year when the cap is already full. He is not denied — his petition is found bona fide, he receives deferred action and a work permit, works legally, and receives his U status when his place in line arrives.

Source: USCIS, U Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

5 · Family members — Supplement A

A U visa can protect your close family too, through Form I-918, Supplement A, filed with your petition or later. If you are 21 or older, you may petition for your spouse and your children. If you are under 21, you may also petition for your parents and your unmarried siblings under 18. Family members must wait until your own I-918 is approved before their derivative U status can be granted, and included family members in the U.S. may also receive deferred action and work authorization through the bona fide determination process. Family members who never held U status may still reach a green card later through Form I-929 after you get yours — an attorney should map that timing, because a family member who does not have derivative U status when you get your green card loses the chance to get it afterward.

Source: USCIS, U Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

6 · After the U visa — work permit and the green card

  • Work permit: the main applicant is employment-authorized with U status, and the work-permit card is issued with the approval — no separate Form I-765 is needed for the principal. Family members in the U.S. file Form I-765 to get their permit card.
  • Green card after 3 years: you may apply on Form I-485 if you have been physically present in the U.S. continuously for at least 3 years while in U status and you have not unreasonably refused to help law enforcement since the U visa was granted. Your qualifying family members file their own I-485s when they meet the requirements.
  • Fees: U nonimmigrants are fee-exempt for all forms through adjustment of status — the I-918, and the related forms on this path, carry no USCIS fee. Confirm on Form G-1055 before filing.

7 · What if I am undocumented, entered without inspection, or have a removal order?

The U visa was written for people in exactly this fear. Being undocumented — even having entered without inspection — does not by itself end a U visa case: the Form I-192 waiver can forgive many grounds of inadmissibility for U applicants. A removal order or a case in immigration court makes everything harder and more urgent, and leaving the U.S. can destroy options — do not leave the U.S. and do not ignore any court date. Get a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited nonprofit immediately — the same day if you have a hearing or a removal order. The four choices below are still yours, but on facts like these, the attorney or DOJ door is the one we recommend first, before anything is filed.

8 · T visa — for victims of human trafficking (Form I-914)

What it is: the T visa (T nonimmigrant status) protects victims of a severe form of human trafficking — being recruited, moved, held, or obtained for labor or services (labor trafficking: involuntary servitude, debt bondage, slavery) or for a commercial sex act (sex trafficking), through force, fraud, or coercion — or any commercial sex act involving someone under 18.

Who qualifies: you may qualify if (1) you are or were a victim of a severe form of trafficking; (2) you are physically present in the U.S. because of the trafficking; (3) you have complied with reasonable requests to help law enforcement investigate or prosecute the trafficking — unless you were under 18 when the trafficking happened or cannot cooperate because of physical or psychological trauma; and (4) you would suffer extreme hardship involving unusual and severe harm if removed from the U.S. Inadmissibility can be waived on Form I-192.

What is needed: Form I-914 with your personal statement describing the trafficking, plus evidence. A law-enforcement declaration (Form I-914, Supplement B) is strong evidence, but unlike the U visa it is not the only way to show cooperation — police reports, court records, communications with law enforcement, affidavits, and other credible evidence can also be submitted. Family members may be included on Supplement A (spouse and unmarried children under 21; if you are under 21, also parents and unmarried siblings under 18 — and certain family members in present danger of retaliation).

What happens: there is no USCIS fee — T applicants are fee-exempt for all forms through adjustment of status. While the I-914 is pending, a bona fide determination can bring deferred action and a work permit (file Form I-765 with the I-914 so it is not delayed). T status lasts 4 years; the main applicant's work permit is issued with the approval. After 3 years of continuous presence in T status — or, if earlier, once the trafficking investigation or prosecution is complete and you were present during it — you may apply for a green card on Form I-485. Help, in more than 200 languages: National Human Trafficking Hotline, 1-888-373-7888, free and confidential, 24/7.

Example: a young man is brought to Florida on promises of farm work; his passport is taken, his pay is withheld “for his debt,” and he is threatened when he tries to leave. That is labor trafficking by fraud and coercion. With an attorney, he files Form I-914 with his statement and the evidence of his cooperation — and while it is pending, a bona fide determination gives him deferred action and a work permit.

Source: USCIS, Victims of Human Trafficking: T Nonimmigrant Status — uscis.gov ↗; U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Immigration Options for Victims of Crime — dhs.gov ↗. General information, not legal advice.

People also ask — U visa & T visa

What are the U visa requirements? Four things: a qualifying crime, substantial physical or mental abuse from it, information about the crime with help given or promised to law enforcement (proven by the signed Supplement B certification), and the crime happened in the U.S. or broke U.S. law.

How long does a U visa take? Honestly, years for many people: only 10,000 principal U visas are granted per year, so a waiting line forms. A bona fide determination can bring deferred action and a work permit while you wait — we will never promise you a fast result.

Does a U visa lead to a green card? Yes. After 3 years of continuous presence in U status (and continued reasonable cooperation), you may apply for a green card on Form I-485. T status has the same 3-year door.

Can I apply for a U visa if I am undocumented? Yes — being undocumented does not by itself end a U case, and Form I-192 can waive many inadmissibility problems. Get an attorney or DOJ nonprofit first, and do not leave the U.S.

What is the difference between VAWA and a U visa? VAWA needs a family relationship — an abusive U.S. citizen or green card holder spouse, parent, or child. A U visa needs a crime and cooperation with law enforcement, whoever committed it. Many domestic-violence cases can fit either or both; an attorney checks which fits you.

What if the police will not sign my certification? Without a signed Supplement B there is no U visa — but an attorney can ask a different authorized agency or official, and can check VAWA, T visa, or asylum instead. Do not pay anyone who promises to “make” an agency sign.

100 people start DIY100 × $25 per form$2,500

Every honest way this platform earns — and what you get for it

  • Membership — $9.80/month or $98/year: full checklists, the full fee calculator, case watch, alerts, and renewal reminders stay on.
  • Review — $99 per form · Review Bundle $399 (all 6 forms): we check your finished form before you mail it. Human Review — $199: a full human clerical check plus the Packet Health Check.

  • Professionals pay monthly — clients never pay this: Document Preparer $49/month · Attorney $99/month · Law Student $35/month · DOJ Nonprofit $24.50 / $49.50/month · Employer Door $49/month.

📬 Why USCIS loves a clean packet

USCIS rejects packets for simple, preventable reasons: wrong edition, wrong fee, blank field, missing signature. A clean packet does not get rejected for those. Our 8-Point Packet Health Check + Pre-Flight Lock stops a packet before it goes out if any of those are wrong: correct edition + correct fee checked twice (I-485 edition 09/18/26 · I-864 edition 08/24/26 · fee checked against Form G-1055 · payment by G-1450 / G-1650 — no paper checks), complete evidence in USCIS order (cover letter, exhibit index, documents in the order USCIS expects), no false documents, ever — and your status explained in honest, plain English, so you stop having to call USCIS to ask what it means.

A plain-English explanation of why clean packets help — NIPTEI is not affiliated with or endorsed by USCIS, and USCIS decides every case.

Questions — answered before you pay

Do you give legal advice?

No. We are non-attorney document preparers — we prepare forms at your direction and do not give legal advice or represent you. If your case needs legal advice, we route you to a licensed attorney or a DOJ-accredited nonprofit.

Is the USCIS fee included?

No. The USCIS government fee is separate — it is paid to USCIS at filing and is never combined with our service fee. Both totals are always shown side by side above.

How fast?

Standard: 5–7 business days. Rush: 2–3 business days. 24-Hour Express: within 24 hours of receiving all your documents. That is preparation time — USCIS processing time is separate and set by USCIS.

What if USCIS sends an RFE?

We help you organize and answer it — Simple and Regular RFEs are handled here (Step 3 above). A Complex RFE or NOID goes to a licensed attorney or DOJ-accredited representative.

Can I pay in 3?

Yes. You can split the service fee into 3 payments at no extra fee — the split is shown on every form and in your checkout summary.
